mainEntity.name: What types of transportation businesses may require specialty insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Specialty transportation includes operations such as non-emergency medical transportation, wheelchair transportation, towing, roadside assistance, passenger shuttle services, and vehicle transportation.  Each business carries different risks involving passengers, vehicles, property, or equipment. Review those operational differences alongside the policy wording and applicable requirements.

mainEntity.name: What insurance should non-emergency medical transportation (NEMT) and wheelchair transportation providers review?

acceptedAnswer.text: NEMT businesses should review commercial auto liability, passenger exposures, general liability, and potentially other coverage related to their services.  Vehicle accessibility equipment, passenger assistance, driver qualifications, and transportation contracts may affect coverage requirements. These operational details should be documented when reviewing policy terms and contracts.

mainEntity.name: What insurance should towing and roadside assistance businesses consider for customers' vehicles?

acceptedAnswer.text: Towing businesses should review commercial auto coverage and protection for customers' vehicles while being towed or held in the business's care.  On-hook towing and garagekeepers coverage are examples of specialized protections that may be relevant. Read the policy definitions, covered activities, and custody arrangements to understand the differences.

mainEntity.name: How do insurance requirements differ for passenger transportation, shuttle services, and commercial delivery operations?

acceptedAnswer.text: Transporting passengers introduces risks and insurance requirements that differ from transporting merchandise or equipment.  Passenger capacity, vehicle configuration, transportation contracts, and applicable regulations can influence the type and amount of coverage required. Check the actual passenger operation, vehicle configuration, contracts, and applicable requirements together.

Understand the main coverage categories.

Use these coverage definitions as a starting point, then explore the guide for your operation. Actual policy terms and business activities determine what applies.

Commercial Auto Liability

Helps protect your business when covered vehicles are involved in accidents that cause injury or property damage.

Physical Damage

Helps protect business vehicles from covered losses such as collision, theft, vandalism, fire, and weather damage.

Passenger Liability

Important for businesses that transport people, including medical transportation, shuttle, church, daycare, limousine, and private services.

General Liability

Helps protect against common business claims that may happen outside normal vehicle operation.

Workers Compensation

Helps protect employees who are injured on the job and supports employer protection where required.

Cargo / Vehicle Transport Coverage

For companies responsible for vehicles, equipment, or property while in care, custody, or transit.

Why specialty transportation businesses need the right insurance.

Specialty transportation businesses are exposed to more than ordinary commercial auto risk. Your operation may involve passengers, contracts, schedules, drivers, vehicle care, medical transportation requirements, or roadside service calls.

Start with your operation’s guide, compare the coverage categories, and use its document checklist to identify questions. The examples explain how a review works; they do not determine coverage or promise an insurance placement.

raw.description: Get help comparing a $75,000 BMC-84 surety bond with a BMC-85 trust fund for FMCSA financial responsibility requirements.
raw.text: BMC-84 Surety Bonds& BMC-85 TrustsGuidance on BMC-84 bonds, BMC-85 trusts, renewals, and FMCSA financial responsibility compliance. Freight Broker Financial ResponsibilityBonds and trustsA BMC-84 surety bond provides financial security for payments owed to shippers or motor carriers when a broker fails to meet its covered transportation obligations. FMCSA requires property and household-goods brokers, and applicable freight forwarders, to maintain $75,000 in financial security through a BMC-84 bond or BMC-85 trust.A BMC-85 is a trust arrangement with an eligible financial institution. It must hold $75,000 in qualifying assets; a trust administration fee is not a substitute for those assets. The provider files the appropriate bond or trust form with FMCSA.The role of trust in transportation complianceCompare the funding obligations as well as the fees. A BMC-85 commits qualifying assets to the trust, which can affect the funds available to run the business.With a BMC-84, an approved applicant generally pays a premium rather than depositing the full bond amount. Underwriting may also require collateral. Review indemnity and reimbursement terms: paying a premium does not eliminate the broker's obligations for covered claims.January 16, 2026 FMCSA changesThe 2026 rules tightened trust asset and provider standards. BMC-85 assets are limited to cash, irrevocable letters of credit from federally insured depository institutions, and U.S. Treasury bonds, and must be convertible to cash within seven calendar days. Loan and finance companies are no longer eligible BMC-85 trustees.The rules also address provider reporting, financial failure and suspension when available security falls below $75,000. Respond promptly to any FMCSA notice and follow the current regulatory procedures. These changes did not replace the $75,000 security requirement.Choosing the right providerBond and trust providers should be financially sound, responsive, and experienced with transportation claims and compliance.Motive helps brokers and transportation businesses review available options. For a side-by-side comparison, read our BMC-84 bond vs. BMC-85 trust guide.Reviewed November 10, 2026. Motive can help customers review their bond needs and available assistance while directing regulatory questions to the appropriate authority. What is the difference between a BMC-84 bond and a BMC-85 trust? A BMC-84 is a surety bond issued by a qualified surety provider. A BMC-85 is a trust fund arrangement established through an eligible financial institution.Both are methods of satisfying the applicable $75,000 federal financial security requirement, but their application processes, financial commitments, and obligations differ. Motive can help customers understand the distinction before choosing an appropriate provider. Does a freight broker have to pay the full $75,000 financial security amount upfront? With a BMC-84 surety bond, an approved applicant generally pays a bond premium rather than depositing the full $75,000 face amount. Premiums vary with underwriting and the applicant's financial profile.A BMC-85 trust requires qualifying financial assets or security under its terms. Motive can help explain these differences so customers understand the potential upfront financial commitment. Can a newly established freight brokerage qualify for a surety bond? A new brokerage may qualify for a BMC-84 surety bond, although approval, premium, and other terms depend on underwriting.Financial history, credit factors, and business details may be considered. acceptedAnswer.text: A BMC-84 is a surety bond used to satisfy federal financial security requirements for certain freight brokers and freight forwarders. Motive can help customers review their bond needs and available assistance while directing regulatory questions to the appropriate authority.

mainEntity.name: What is a BMC-84 surety bond, and which transportation businesses need one?

acceptedAnswer.text: A BMC-84 is a surety bond issued by a qualified surety provider. A BMC-85 is a trust fund arrangement established through an eligible financial institution. Both are methods of satisfying the applicable $75,000 federal financial security requirement, but their application processes, financial commitments, and obligations differ. Motive can help customers understand the distinction before choosing an appropriate provider.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between a BMC-84 bond and a BMC-85 trust?

acceptedAnswer.text: With a BMC-84 surety bond, an approved applicant generally pays a bond premium rather than depositing the full $75,000 face amount. Premiums vary with underwriting and the applicant's financial profile. A BMC-85 trust requires qualifying financial assets or security under its terms. Motive can help explain these differences so customers understand the potential upfront financial commitment.

mainEntity.name: Does a freight broker have to pay the full $75,000 financial security amount upfront?

acceptedAnswer.text: A new brokerage may qualify for a BMC-84 surety bond, although approval, premium, and other terms depend on underwriting. Financial history, credit factors, and business details may be considered. Motive can help new freight brokers understand the application information they may need and explore available bond assistance.

nojs.mainText:
BMC-84 Surety Bonds& BMC-85 Trusts

Guidance on BMC-84 bonds, BMC-85 trusts, renewals, and FMCSA financial responsibility compliance.

Freight Broker Financial Responsibility
Bonds and trusts

A BMC-84 surety bond provides financial security for payments owed to shippers or motor carriers when a broker fails to meet its covered transportation obligations. FMCSA requires property and household-goods brokers, and applicable freight forwarders, to maintain $75,000 in financial security through a BMC-84 bond or BMC-85 trust.

A BMC-85 is a trust arrangement with an eligible financial institution. It must hold $75,000 in qualifying assets; a trust administration fee is not a substitute for those assets. The provider files the appropriate bond or trust form with FMCSA.

The role of trust in transportation compliance

Compare the funding obligations as well as the fees. A BMC-85 commits qualifying assets to the trust, which can affect the funds available to run the business.

With a BMC-84, an approved applicant generally pays a premium rather than depositing the full bond amount. Underwriting may also require collateral. Review indemnity and reimbursement terms: paying a premium does not eliminate the broker's obligations for covered claims.

January 16, 2026 FMCSA changes

The 2026 rules tightened trust asset and provider standards. BMC-85 assets are limited to cash, irrevocable letters of credit from federally insured depository institutions, and U.S. Treasury bonds, and must be convertible to cash within seven calendar days. Loan and finance companies are no longer eligible BMC-85 trustees.

The rules also address provider reporting, financial failure and suspension when available security falls below $75,000. Respond promptly to any FMCSA notice and follow the current regulatory procedures. These changes did not replace the $75,000 security requirement.

Choosing the right provider

Bond and trust providers should be financially sound, responsive, and experienced with transportation claims and compliance.

Motive helps brokers and transportation businesses review available options. For a side-by-side comparison, read our BMC-84 bond vs. BMC-85 trust guide.

Reviewed November 10, 2026. Sources: FMCSA rule overview, FMCSA filing requirements, and current 49 CFR 387.307.

raw.title: Medical Courier Insurance | Commercial Auto, Cargo & Liability | Motive Insurance
raw.description: Starting or operating a medical courier service? Motive Insurance helps review commercial auto, cargo, liability, cyber, E&O and contract insurance requirements for medical delivery, lab specimens and pharmaceutical courier operations.
h1: Medical Courier Insurance Built Around the Contracts You Want to Win
raw.text: Medical Courier Insurance Built Around the Contracts You Want to WinBring Motive the route requirements before you sign the contract.Start My Review → Laboratory specimensPharmaceutical deliveriesMedical supplies & equipmentDedicated healthcare routes Before the first pickupBefore You Accept the Route, Understand the RiskA medical courier contract can make a small business look ready to grow overnight. But the insurance exhibit may require coverage that your current auto policy, general liability policy or certificate does not provide.What you carry matters. A box of disposable supplies, a temperature-sensitive medication and an irreplaceable laboratory specimen create different exposures. A missed delivery window may also create a financial loss that is separate from damage to the shipment itself.Start with the actual work: who owns the vehicles, who drives them, what travels inside and who is responsible when something goes wrong. Then compare those facts with the contract and policy wording.A certificate is a starting point.A certificate of insurance summarizes coverage; it does not change policy terms or add endorsements. Contract requirements need to be checked against the coverage actually in place. The Motive differenceMotive Contract-Ready Coverage ReviewMedical courier businesses should understand the insurance requirements connected to the contracts they are trying to win. Bring the proposed route requirements to Motive so we can help organize the insurance questions before you commit.01 / UNDERSTANDStart with the operationReview delivery types, vehicles, drivers, territory, cargo values and handling practices. Tell us about subcontractors, personal vehicles and any planned changes.02 / COMPARERead the insurance requirementsDiscuss requested limits, coverage types, additional insured wording and other insurance provisions. Identify requirements that need clarification from the client or insurer.03 / PREPAREBuild the coverage conversationReview available options, relevant exclusions and documentation needs. Coverage placement, endorsements and client acceptance remain subject to review and approval. A coverage plan for your operationCoverage Medical Courier Businesses May NeedMedical courier insurance is usually a combination of policies. The right mix depends on your deliveries, driver model and written agreements. No single coverage automatically protects every vehicle, shipment, service error or privacy event.Commercial autoGeneral liabilityCargo / inland marineE&OCyber / privacyHired & non-owned autoWorkers’ compensationUmbrella / excess 01 / ON THE ROADCommercial AutoCommercial auto liability addresses covered bodily injury and property damage claims arising from business vehicle use. Physical damage coverage may help repair or replace an insured vehicle after a covered loss, subject to deductibles and terms.Tell the insurer that you perform medical courier work. Vehicle type alone does not describe the exposure, and a personal auto policy may restrict or exclude delivery use. Confirm the vehicles, drivers and operating territory included in the policy.Contract review: Check the required liability limit, owned-vehicle coverage and any hired or non-owned auto requirements. Explore commercial van insurance. 02 / AT THE DELIVERY LOCATIONGeneral LiabilityGeneral liability may respond to covered third-party injury or property damage claims involving your business operations, such as an accident during a pickup at a client location.It generally does not replace commercial auto liability, professional liability or insurance for goods in your care. Review those exposures separately, including loading and unloading situations where policy wording matters.Contract review: Compare occurrence and aggregate limits and requested additional insured endorsements. Learn about general liability. 03 / WHAT YOU CARRYCargo / Inland MarineCargo or an appropriate inland marine policy may address covered loss or damage to property you transport. Standard cargo forms may exclude or limit pharmaceuticals, biological materials, contamination, spoilage or changes in temperature.Explain the highest value in a vehicle at one time, not only the value of an average delivery. A specimen’s testing or recollection cost may differ from its insurable value. Discuss valuation, theft restrictions, unattended vehicles and refrigeration breakdown explicitly.Contract review: Confirm covered commodities, valuation, deductibles and any temperature or spoilage endorsements; do not assume “cargo coverage” includes every medical shipment. 04 / THE SERVICE YOU PROVIDEProfessional Liability / Errors & OmissionsA misdelivery, missed deadline or failure to follow a service instruction can lead to a claim for financial loss. Professional liability, also called errors and omissions (E&O), may address certain covered service-related allegations.Medical courier activities must fit the policy’s description of professional services. Delays, contractual penalties, spoilage and other losses may be excluded or restricted. A contractual promise to reimburse a client is not automatically an insured loss.Contract review: Discuss the specific services, retroactive date, claims-reporting conditions and exclusions before relying on E&O to satisfy a contract. 05 / SENSITIVE INFORMATIONCyber / Privacy LiabilityDelivery apps, manifests, scanned documents and driver devices may contain sensitive information. Cyber and privacy coverage may provide specified breach response services or liability protection after a covered incident.Coverage varies for lost paper records, employee mistakes, third-party platforms and electronic data. Explain what information your business receives, stores and accesses, and how drivers use personal devices.Contract review: Separate the client’s privacy obligations from insurance requirements. Cyber insurance does not establish HIPAA compliance. 06 / VEHICLES YOU DO NOT OWNHired & Non-Owned AutoIf you rent a replacement van or employees use their own cars for deliveries, your business may need hired and non-owned auto liability. These coverages address specified liability exposures involving vehicles your business does not own.They do not automatically cover damage to those vehicles or replace a driver’s own insurance. Contractor arrangements and vehicle leasing structures need individual review; the coverage does not automatically extend to every subcontractor.Contract review: Identify who owns, leases and dispatches each vehicle, and whether the contract permits independent contractor drivers. 07 / THE PEOPLE ON YOUR TEAMWorkers’ CompensationWorkers’ compensation provides benefits for covered work-related employee injuries or illnesses under applicable state law. Lifting, vehicle accidents and repetitive delivery tasks are relevant exposures for courier teams.Calling a driver an independent contractor does not by itself settle their status under the applicable rules. Review the actual working arrangement, states of operation and any client requirements with appropriate advisers.Contract review: Discuss workers’ compensation, employers liability limits and any waiver-of-subrogation request. Explore workers’ compensation coverage. 08 / ADDITIONAL LIABILITY LIMITSUmbrella / ExcessUmbrella or excess liability can add limits above specified underlying liability policies. It may help address a client’s higher limit requirements, depending on the policies and endorsements involved.Confirm which policies are scheduled underneath it and how exclusions apply. An umbrella does not automatically extend cargo, E&O or cyber coverage, and additional limits do not remove exclusions in the underlying program.Contract review: Check whether the client accepts an excess structure, the required underlying limits and whether additional insured status extends as requested. Coverage + operational disciplineMedical Courier Compliance MattersInsurance is one part of route readiness. Your operation also needs procedures suited to the shipments you accept: packaging verification, chain of custody, delivery records, spill response, driver instruction and temperature controls where relevant.Assign responsibility for each step with the customer. Confirm who classifies and packages shipments, supplies handling instructions, monitors temperature and responds when a package is damaged or a delivery is delayed.UN3373 / Specimen Transport OverviewUN3373 identifies Biological substance, Category B. Not every medical specimen falls into this classification. The classification determines the applicable transport requirements; Category A substances and exempt specimens are treated differently.Category B packaging generally involves a primary receptacle, secondary packaging and rigid outer packaging, with additional leakproof, absorbent and marking requirements as applicable. The correct preparation depends on the material and transport conditions. Medical Courier Insurance Built Around the Contracts You Want to Win

Bring Motive the route requirements before you sign the contract.

Start My Review
→
Laboratory specimens
Pharmaceutical deliveries
Medical supplies & equipment
Dedicated healthcare routes
BEFORE THE FIRST PICKUP
Before You Accept the Route, Understand the Risk

A medical courier contract can make a small business look ready to grow overnight. But the insurance exhibit may require coverage that your current auto policy, general liability policy or certificate does not provide.

What you carry matters. A box of disposable supplies, a temperature-sensitive medication and an irreplaceable laboratory specimen create different exposures. A missed delivery window may also create a financial loss that is separate from damage to the shipment itself.

Start with the actual work: who owns the vehicles, who drives them, what travels inside and who is responsible when something goes wrong. Then compare those facts with the contract and policy wording.

A certificate is a starting point.

A certificate of insurance summarizes coverage; it does not change policy terms or add endorsements. Contract requirements need to be checked against the coverage actually in place.

THE MOTIVE DIFFERENCE
Motive Contract-Ready Coverage Review

Medical courier businesses should understand the insurance requirements connected to the contracts they are trying to win. Bring the proposed route requirements to Motive so we can help organize the insurance questions before you commit.

01 / UNDERSTAND
Start with the operation

Review delivery types, vehicles, drivers, territory, cargo values and handling practices. Tell us about subcontractors, personal vehicles and any planned changes.

02 / COMPARE
Read the insurance requirements

Discuss requested limits, coverage types, additional insured wording and other insurance provisions. Identify requirements that need clarification from the client or insurer.

03 / PREPARE
Build the coverage conversation

Review available options, relevant exclusions and documentation needs. Coverage placement, endorsements and client acceptance remain subject to review and approval.

A COVERAGE PLAN FOR YOUR OPERATION
Coverage Medical Courier Businesses May Need

Medical courier insurance is usually a combination of policies. The right mix depends on your deliveries, driver model and written agreements. No single coverage automatically protects every vehicle, shipment, service error or privacy event.

Commercial auto
General liability
Cargo / inland marine
E&O
Cyber / privacy
Hired & non-owned auto
Workers’ compensation
Umbrella / excess
01 / ON THE ROAD
Commercial Auto

Commercial auto liability addresses covered bodily injury and property damage claims arising from business vehicle use. Physical damage coverage may help repair or replace an insured vehicle after a covered loss, subject to deductibles and terms.

Tell the insurer that you perform medical courier work. Vehicle type alone does not describe the exposure, and a personal auto policy may restrict or exclude delivery use. Confirm the vehicles, drivers and operating territory included in the policy.

Contract review: Check the required liability limit, owned-vehicle coverage and any hired or non-owned auto requirements. Explore commercial van insurance.

02 / AT THE DELIVERY LOCATION
General Liability

General liability may respond to covered third-party injury or property damage claims involving your business operations, such as an accident during a pickup at a client location.

It generally does not replace commercial auto liability, professional liability or insurance for goods in your care. Review those exposures separately, including loading and unloading situations where policy wording matters.

Contract review: Compare occurrence and aggregate limits and requested additional insured endorsements. Learn about general liability.

03 / WHAT YOU CARRY
Cargo / Inland Marine

Cargo or an appropriate inland marine policy may address covered loss or damage to property you transport. Standard cargo forms may exclude or limit pharmaceuticals, biological materials, contamination, spoilage or changes in temperature.

Explain the highest value in a vehicle at one time, not only the value of an average delivery. A specimen’s testing or recollection cost may differ from its insurable value. Discuss valuation, theft restrictions, unattended vehicles and refrigeration breakdown explicitly.

Contract review: Confirm covered commodities, valuation, deductibles and any temperature or spoilage endorsements; do not assume “cargo coverage” includes every medical shipment.

04 / THE SERVICE YOU PROVIDE
Professional Liability / Errors & Omissions

A misdelivery, missed deadline or failure to follow a service instruction can lead to a claim for financial loss. Professional liability, also called errors and omissions (E&O), may address certain covered service-related allegations.

Medical courier activities must fit the policy’s description of professional services. Delays, contractual penalties, spoilage and other losses may be excluded or restricted. A contractual promise to reimburse a client is not automatically an insured loss.

Contract review: Discuss the specific services, retroactive date, claims-reporting conditions and exclusions before relying on E&O to satisfy a contract.

05 / SENSITIVE INFORMATION
Cyber / Privacy Liability

Delivery apps, manifests, scanned documents and driver devices may contain sensitive information. Cyber and privacy coverage may provide specified breach response services or liability protection after a covered incident.

Coverage varies for lost paper records, employee mistakes, third-party platforms and electronic data. Explain what information your business receives, stores and accesses, and how drivers use personal devices.

Contract review: Separate the client’s privacy obligations from insurance requirements. Cyber insurance does not establish HIPAA compliance.

06 / VEHICLES YOU DO NOT OWN
Hired & Non-Owned Auto

If you rent a replacement van or employees use their own cars for deliveries, your business may need hired and non-owned auto liability. These coverages address specified liability exposures involving vehicles your business does not own.

They do not automatically cover damage to those vehicles or replace a driver’s own insurance. Contractor arrangements and vehicle leasing structures need individual review; the coverage does not automatically extend to every subcontractor.

Contract review: Identify who owns, leases and dispatches each vehicle, and whether the contract permits independent contractor drivers.

07 / THE PEOPLE ON YOUR TEAM
Workers’ Compensation

Workers’ compensation provides benefits for covered work-related employee injuries or illnesses under applicable state law. Lifting, vehicle accidents and repetitive delivery tasks are relevant exposures for courier teams.

Calling a driver an independent contractor does not by itself settle their status under the applicable rules. Review the actual working arrangement, states of operation and any client requirements with appropriate advisers.

Contract review: Discuss workers’ compensation, employers liability limits and any waiver-of-subrogation request. Explore workers’ compensation coverage.

08 / ADDITIONAL LIABILITY LIMITS
Umbrella / Excess

Umbrella or excess liability can add limits above specified underlying liability policies. It may help address a client’s higher limit requirements, depending on the policies and endorsements involved.

Confirm which policies are scheduled underneath it and how exclusions apply. An umbrella does not automatically extend cargo, E&O or cyber coverage, and additional limits do not remove exclusions in the underlying program.

Contract review: Check whether the client accepts an excess structure, the required underlying limits and whether additional insured status extends as requested.

COVERAGE + OPERATIONAL DISCIPLINE
Medical Courier Compliance Matters

Insurance is one part of route readiness. Your operation also needs procedures suited to the shipments you accept: packaging verification, chain of custody, delivery records, spill response, driver instruction and temperature controls where relevant.

Assign responsibility for each step with the customer. Confirm who classifies and packages shipments, supplies handling instructions, monitors temperature and responds when a package is damaged or a delivery is delayed.

UN3373 / Specimen Transport Overview

UN3373 identifies Biological substance, Category B. Not every medical specimen falls into this classification. The classification determines the applicable transport requirements; Category A substances and exempt specimens are treated differently.

Category B packaging generally involves a primary receptacle, secondary packaging and rigid outer packaging, with additional leakproof, absorbent and marking requirements as applicable. The correct preparation depends on the material and transport conditions. This overview is not a packaging checklist or a training certification.

Confirm classification and packaging responsibilities with the shipper, and verify the current rules before accepting specimens. Review PHMSA’s infectious-substance guidance.

HIPAA: Understanding the Conduit Explanation

HHS explains that certain couriers acting only as conduits for protected health information are not business associates. The exception is narrow: access is random or infrequent as needed to perform transport, and any storage is incidental to transmission.

A business that routinely accesses or maintains protected health information may have different obligations. Your use of delivery software, retained records and customer data needs its own review. Being a medical courier does not automatically establish conduit status.

Review the actual services and any business associate agreement with qualified counsel. Read HHS’s courier and conduit explanation.

Cold-chain requirements deserve a separate conversation.

Explain packaging, temperature ranges, monitoring, backup equipment and loss-response procedures to the insurer. Temperature control alone does not mean a spoilage or contamination claim is covered.

FIND YOUR NEXT STEP
Medical Courier Contract Readiness Check

Choose the stage that best describes your business for a recommended next step. This is a planning guide, not an insurance approval or compliance certification. Your selection does not submit a review request.

Building the Operation

STAGE 2
Pursuing Contracts
You are talking to clients and comparing route opportunities.
STAGE 3
Route Ready
You have an offer and need to confirm insurance details.
STAGE 4
Scaling the Fleet
You are adding drivers, vehicles, customers or territory.
Build your insurance brief.

Outline your delivery type, service area, vehicles and driver model. Ask prospective clients for their insurance requirements before committing to a route or vehicle.

AN OPPORTUNITY ON THE TABLE?
Already Have a Contract Offer?

Bring Motive the route requirements before you sign the contract. A proposed agreement, insurance exhibit and clear description of the deliveries give us a more useful starting point than a limit alone.

We can help you review the insurance provisions and discuss coverage options. Your client determines whether your documentation meets its requirements; Motive’s review does not guarantee a contract award.

FROM YOUR FIRST ROUTE TO YOUR NEXT FLEET
Who We Help

Tell Motive what you transport and how you operate. Coverage availability depends on the business, commodities, underwriting and location.

Medical courier businesses

Independent operators and established businesses moving healthcare deliveries between clinics, hospitals and other facilities.

Specimen transport operations

Couriers carrying laboratory samples with specific pickup windows, handling instructions and documentation requirements.

Laboratory courier companies

Dedicated lab routes and multi-driver operations coordinating repeated pickups and time-sensitive deliveries.

Pharmaceutical delivery businesses

Operators transporting medications with cargo values, theft exposures and temperature requirements that need careful review.

Medical supply & equipment couriers

Businesses moving supplies and equipment, including high-value items or deliveries that involve additional handling services.

Growing healthcare delivery fleets

Teams adding vehicles, drivers, subcontractors, service areas or new client agreements.

ILLINOIS MEDICAL COURIER INSURANCE
Local Perspective. Contract-Focused Coverage.

From Chicago-area healthcare routes to deliveries across Illinois, describe the full territory your business serves. Urban stops, longer trips, overnight parking and cross-state deliveries can all matter to underwriting.

Motive Insurance has locations in Matteson and Wood Dale. We help businesses discuss the insurance side of their operation, including commercial vehicles, liability and employee exposures.

Planning routes beyond Illinois?

Tell us where vehicles are garaged, where drivers work and whether you cross into Indiana, Wisconsin or other states. Coverage availability and applicable requirements need to be reviewed for the actual operation.

Keep business licensing, motor carrier authority and transport requirements separate from your insurance review; buying a policy does not establish operating authority.

raw.title: Box Truck Operating Costs: A Matteson Owner’s Guide
raw.description: Starting a box truck business in Matteson? Understand fuel, deadhead miles, detention, insurance, and the numbers behind a profitable operation.
raw.text: Box TruckOperating Costsin MattesonGet the Weekly Worksheet The load payment is revenue. Your earnings are what remain after the business pays its bills. When reviewing insurance as an operating expense, use our box truck insurance quote preparation guide to prepare consistent details for comparing coverage. Before you leave a warehouse job, finance a truck, or accept your first delivery, answer one question: How much does this business need to bring in to pay its expenses—and pay you? For a prospective box truck owner-operator in Matteson, a weekly revenue screenshot leaves too much unanswered. It doesn’t show empty return trips, loading delays, repair bills, insurance payments, or invoices that haven’t been collected. This guide explains how to evaluate those costs before committing your savings. 01 / Owner guideWhat does it cost to operate a box truck? Box truck operating costs include fuel, maintenance, tires, insurance, truck payments or depreciation, parking, tolls, registration, business administration, and any employees or contractors. Your actual costs depend on the truck and the operation. A local delivery business and an interstate freight business should not use the same budget simply because both operate a 26-foot box truck. Separate your expenses into three groups: Cost group What to include Why it matters Recurring costs Insurance, truck payment, parking, software, bookkeeping These bills can continue during a slow week. Operating costs Fuel, tolls, maintenance, tires, delivery-related charges These change with mileage, usage, and the work accepted. Reserves and owner compensation Repair reserve, replacement savings, taxes, and payment for your work Cash left in the account is not automatically available to spend. Avoid counting the same expense twice. For example, a cash-flow budget tracks loan payments, while an accounting profit calculation treats financing and depreciation differently. An accountant can help establish the right method. 02 / Owner guideHow deadhead miles reduce box truck revenue per mile Empty miles still use fuel, time, and equipment. Include them in the cost of the complete trip. Deadhead miles are miles driven without a paying load. They can include traveling to a pickup, repositioning after delivery, or returning to your operating base. Here is a worked example—not an actual load listing or a claim about available Matteson freight rates: A customer pays $640 for a delivery covering 200 loaded miles. Trip outcome Total miles Gross revenue per total mile Count only the loaded movement 200 $3.20 Add 100 unpaid miles 300 $2.13 Return empty another 200 miles 400 $1.60 The payment never changed. The amount of driving required to earn it did. Calculate revenue against all miles the job creates. Then subtract expenses. A load that looks attractive on loaded mileage alone can look very different after the return trip. A possible return load should remain a possibility in your budget until it is booked. 03 / Owner guideWhat fuel can take out of a load payment The U.S. Energy Information Administration reported an average Midwest on-highway diesel price of $6.259 per gallon for the week of October 12, 2026. This is a dated regional benchmark, not a price quote from a Matteson fuel station. Source: EIA diesel fuel prices Using that benchmark, a 400-mile trip produces the following calculation: Assumed fuel economy Fuel required Estimated fuel expense 8 miles per gallon 50 gallons $312.95 10 miles per gallon 40 gallons $250.36 12 miles per gallon Approximately 33.33 gallons $208.63 These fuel-economy figures are calculation assumptions, not specifications for your truck. In the 10-mpg example, $640 in revenue becomes $389.64 after fuel alone. Insurance, maintenance, tolls, truck ownership costs, and compensation for the operator still need to come out. Use fuel receipts and measured mileage to build your own numbers. If your truck runs on gasoline, use gasoline prices rather than this diesel benchmark. 04 / Owner guideLoading delays affect more than your schedule A delivery can occupy your truck even while the odometer is barely moving. FMCSA summarizes a 2014 study that found detention at approximately one in ten stops, with an average 1.4 hours beyond a two-hour loading and unloading threshold. These are historical commercial-trucking findings, not a current estimate for Matteson box truck operators. Source: FMCSA detention research For your business, the important questions are practical: What appointment time have you agreed to? When does billable detention begin under the agreement? What arrival and departure evidence is required? Who authorizes additional charges? What happens if the delay prevents your next pickup? Record detention requested, approved, and paid separately. An additional charge on an invoice is not collected income. 05 / Owner guideHow much should you budget for box truck insurance? Use a quote based on your operation rather than another operator’s premium. Progressive identifies truck size, cargo, driving records, operating distance and location, coverage limits, and deductibles as factors affecting box truck insurance costs. Its guidance does not establish one price that applies to every box truck business. Source: Progressive Commercial Prepare these details before discussing coverage: The truck’s VIN, value, ownership, and financing information. Drivers and their driving histories. What you transport and the value of the goods. Typical routes, operating radius, and garaging location. Customer contracts and requested insurance limits. Your existing policy and renewal documents, if applicable. Compare more than the monthly payment. Review total premium, payment terms, limits, deductibles, exclusions, and whether the proposed coverage matches the work. Motive helps trucking businesses review vehicles, drivers, cargo, operating radius, contracts, and budget when considering coverage options. Explore Motive truck insurance 06 / Owner guideThe Box Truck Week-in-Review Worksheet Review receipts, mileage, invoices, and collected payments together at the end of each week. Print / save worksheet as PDFWeek of: __________________ Truck: __________________ Before expanding—or deciding the business can replace your job—close each week with a consistent record. Record What to enter Revenue billed Completed work invoiced during the week Cash collected Payments actually received, including earlier invoices Loaded miles Miles driven while carrying paying freight Empty miles Pickup travel, repositioning, and empty returns Fuel expense Actual fuel purchases Other trip expenses Tolls, parking, and job-specific charges Recurring cost allocation A consistent weekly share of recurring business costs Maintenance and reserves Actual repairs and separately identified reserve contributions Owner hours Driving, loading, dispatching, paperwork, and collections Calculate: Gross revenue per total mile = revenue billed ÷ total miles Deadhead percentage = empty miles ÷ total miles × 100 Operating cash movement = cash collected − cash paid out These figures answer different questions. Revenue per mile measures the work. Cash movement shows what happened to the bank balance. Neither, by itself, proves the business earned enough to pay the owner. 07 / Owner guideIs a box truck business profitable? It can be, but profitability depends on the relationship between collected revenue, operating expenses, truck ownership costs, and the work required to earn that revenue. Before leaving employment, compare the business with your current situation: What compensation would be available for your work? How many total hours would you spend earning it? What benefits would you need to replace? Could the business meet its obligations during repairs or slow collections? Would money remain for maintenance and eventual truck replacement? The goal is to build a business that can pay you consistently while remaining able to operate. 08 / Owner guideFrequently asked questions Should I calculate rates using loaded miles or total miles? Use total miles to evaluate the complete movement. Loaded-mile pricing can be useful for comparing offers, but it does not capture unpaid travel. Is money left after fuel my profit? No. Fuel is only one expense. Account for the remaining operating costs, recurring obligations, and the cost of your own work. Can another operator’s insurance payment tell me what mine will cost? It can provide context, but it cannot replace a quote. Differences in vehicles, drivers, cargo, routes, limits, and deductibles can affect pricing. What records should I keep from my first week? Keep load agreements, delivery records, invoices, payment records, mileage logs, fuel receipts, other expense receipts, and loading-delay documentation. 09 / Owner guideReview your coverage before committing to the work Bring Motive the details of the operation you plan to run: your truck, drivers, freight, routes, and customer requirements. Discuss box truck coverage with Motive Insurance 4801 Southwick Dr, Suite 270 Matteson, IL 60443 888-943-0888 Explore box truck coverage Call 888-943-0888 Educational information. Calculations are illustrative and do not represent actual customer earnings, available freight rates, or an insurance quote.

Box Truck
Insurance Quote

Prepare your details. Take the next step with Motive.

Request My Quote ↗Call 888-943-0888
Know what to prepare

Your truck has a job to do. Start your quote with the details that describe it.

Prepare your vehicle, cargo, operating area, and driver information, then request a quote through Motive’s Trucking Insurance form.

Whether you are arranging coverage or comparing options, accurate information gives the conversation a useful starting point.

The quick answer

What do you need for a box truck insurance quote?

Motive’s trucking form asks about your business, where the truck is kept, the loads you carry, how far you drive, your vehicle, and your coverage needs.

Gather those details before starting. Check identifying numbers and addresses carefully, and contact Motive if you are unsure how a question applies.

01 / Get ready

Prepare your information before you start
Contact and business information
Garaging location
Cargo and operating radius
Vehicle details
Driver information
Coverage information
Check the details against the vehicle you want insured.
01
Contact and business information

Have your personal and business details available, along with a phone number and email where Motive can reach you. Review your entries before submitting.

02
Garaging location

Use the location where the vehicle is actually kept. The form requests the parking ZIP code and garaging address.

03
Cargo and operating radius

Describe the loads you transport and select the radius that reflects your operation. If the available choices do not clearly fit your work, speak with Motive before guessing.

04
Vehicle details

Have your truck’s VIN available and review the vehicle-value question. Make sure the information describes the truck you want insured.

05
Driver information

Prepare your driver’s license information and complete the applicable driver questions. Include CDL details where requested and relevant.

06
Coverage information

Review the coverage selections, cargo entries, current-insurance question, and other applicable items in the form.

Submitting your preferences starts a request. It does not establish that insurance is in place.

Request My Quote ↗

02 / Know the differences

Understand what you are comparing

A box truck insurance conversation can involve different types of protection. Confirm which coverages are included rather than assuming one selection protects the entire operation.

Coverage comparison: what to review with your agent
Coverage	What to review
Automobile liability	Liability arising from operating the truck, subject to policy terms
Comprehensive and collision	Physical damage protection for the insured vehicle, including applicable deductibles
Motor cargo	Protection for transported goods, including covered commodities, limits, exclusions, and conditions

Coverage needs and availability depend on the operation and insurer underwriting.

Explore Motive’s commercial truck insurance coverage.

03 / One last review

Before you submit your quote request
Check your contact information.
Confirm the vehicle and driver identification entries.
Use the actual garaging location.
Describe your loads accurately.
Select the operating radius that fits your work.
Review the applicable coverage entries.
Have a question? Call Motive at 888-943-0888.

Look beyond the number

Compare more than the payment

When reviewing quotes, compare the operation described, coverage limits, deductibles, exclusions, and payment terms.

A lower payment deserves a closer look if the quotes use different vehicle details or provide different protection. Ask an agent to explain material differences before making your decision.

raw.text: Moving company insurance · BMC-34 support Household Goods Motor Carrier Insurance Coverage and BMC-34 filings for moving companies that transport household goods. Moving household goods creates a different insurance responsibility than simply operating a commercial vehicle. Motive helps household goods motor carriers understand the coverage and filings required around the way they operate. Commercial auto. Cargo. Liability. BMC-34 filings. One insurance conversation. Get a Household Goods Insurance QuoteAsk About a BMC-34 Filing → For the truck, the cargo, and every move. Commercial autoHousehold goods cargoBusiness liabilityBMC-34 filing support Built around your operationWhat is a Household Goods Motor Carrier?A Household Goods Motor Carrier is a for-hire moving company that transports household goods for the public.For interstate operations, household goods motor carriers have insurance and operating authority requirements that differ from many other commercial transportation businesses.More than getting from A to B.Packing and unpackingLoading and unloadingInventorying household goodsBinding or nonbinding estimatesTransportation between homes or other eligible locations Protect every part of the moveInsurance Built for Moving CompaniesYour business may be responsible for the truck, the driver, the crew, and your customer’s property. The right insurance program starts with the way you work.Commercial AutoCoverage for covered bodily injury, property damage and vehicle exposures involving your moving trucks and vans.Motor Truck CargoCoverage for covered loss or damage to customers’ household goods while your business transports them.Public LiabilityBodily injury and property damage liability protection arising from commercial vehicle operations.General LiabilityProtection for certain third-party claims from business operations outside the normal auto exposure.Workers’ CompensationCoverage related to employee injuries, including the physically demanding work of moving crews.Physical DamageProtection for insured vehicles against covered collision and comprehensive losses.Umbrella or Excess LiabilityAdditional liability protection above certain underlying policies, when appropriate.Property or Storage ExposureCoverage to review when your business has a warehouse or stores customers’ property. Coverage → filing → federal recordWhat Is a BMC-34 Filing?A BMC-34 is proof of cargo liability insurance filed with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration for qualifying household goods motor carriers.01 / THE COVERAGECargo PolicyThe actual insurance coverage for covered household goods cargo losses.02 / THE PROOFBMC-34Proof of qualifying cargo coverage, submitted by the insurer or authorized electronic filer.03 / THE RECORDFMCSAThe filing becomes part of the carrier’s federal insurance and operating authority record.A BMC-34 is not a separate insurance policy. It is the filing that shows the required cargo liability insurance is in place. Motive can help coordinate the insurance side of that process.Ask About a BMC-34 Filing → The connection to your authorityWhy Does the BMC-34 Matter?Qualifying interstate household goods carriers need proof of cargo insurance on file with FMCSA. Missing required insurance filings can affect obtaining or maintaining operating authority.That makes the filing more than paperwork. It connects the policy to your federal insurance record.Three details to confirmPOLICYRequired cargo coverage is in placeFILINGThe insurer has submitted the applicable filingAUTHORITYFMCSA’s record reflects the required proof See the whole insurance pictureBMC-34 Is Only One Part of the Insurance PictureThe filing addresses proof of cargo liability insurance. It does not replace the other coverage your moving business may need.Coverage and filing responsibilities for a moving-company insurance reviewCoverage to reviewWhat it addressesBMC-34 connectionMotor truck cargoCustomers’ household goods in transitProof of qualifying cargo coverageCommercial auto / public liabilityCommercial vehicle liability exposuresSeparate liability filing where applicableGeneral liabilityCertain third-party business liability claimsNot established by BMC-34Workers’ compensationEmployee injuriesNot established by BMC-34Physical damageCovered loss to insured vehiclesNot established by BMC-34Umbrella / excessAdditional liability limits over underlying policiesNot established by BMC-34Storage / propertyWarehouse and stored-property exposuresSeparate coverage review needed Different proof. Different responsibility.BMC-34 vs. Public Liability FilingBMC-34Cargo liability insuranceHousehold goods cargo exposureFederal cargo insurance filingPublic Liability FilingBodily injury and property damage financial responsibilityCommercial vehicle liability exposureSeparate federal insurance filing where applicableA qualifying household goods carrier may have both public liability and cargo filing requirements. Motive helps connect those filings to the insurance program. Start with your operating authorityWho May Need a BMC-34?A BMC-34 is particularly relevant to businesses operating as household goods motor carriers under applicable interstate authority.Not every business delivering furniture or appliances is automatically a household goods motor carrier. Your business model and operating authority matter.Review My Operation →Interstate household goods moversMoving companies with applicable household goods authorityBusinesses transporting customers’ household goods between states Personal belongings. Specialized risks.Moving Companies Have Different Risks Than General Freight CarriersYour crew enters customers’ homes, carries furniture through hallways, uses loading ramps, and handles belongings that may be packed, transported, temporarily stored, and unloaded.A damage claim can involve more than the truck itself. Your insurance should reflect that reality. Prepare for your quoteWhat Motive Will Want to KnowHave these details handy. They help us understand what your insurance program needs to accomplish.Number of moving trucksVehicle types and weightsNumber of driversNumber of moving crewsLocal or interstate operationsStates where you operateOperating radiusHousehold goods transportedPacking and unpacking servicesLoading and unloading servicesWarehouse or storage operationsCurrent cargo coverageCurrent auto coverageClaims historyFMCSA operating authorityCurrent insurance filingsRenewal date From first truck to first moveStarting a New Household Goods Moving Company?Build the insurance and filing process together, so required filings are part of the plan from the beginning.01Understand the operationDescribe your vehicles, crews, territory, and moving services.02Review required coverageDiscuss the policies and limits your operation may need.03Identify applicable filingsConnect cargo and public liability requirements to your authority.04Place coverageWork through underwriting and confirm policy terms and effective dates.05Complete applicable filingsCoordinate with the insurer or authorized electronic filer.06Begin operationsConfirm active authority and all other operating requirements before your first move. Room to growGrowing Moving FleetsOne truck has different insurance needs than twenty. Each new vehicle, driver, and crew can change your exposure.One truckSmall fleetGrowing operationEstablished fleetClaims, vehicle schedules, certificates, contracts, and insurance administration become more complex as you grow. Motive helps bring those pieces into one conversation.Explore commercial truck and fleet coverage → Your questions, answeredHousehold Goods Insurance & BMC-34 FAQsWhat is a BMC-34 filing?A BMC-34 is proof of cargo liability insurance filed with FMCSA for qualifying household goods motor carriers. It connects the required cargo coverage to the carrier’s federal insurance record.Who needs a BMC-34 filing?It is relevant to household goods motor carriers operating under applicable interstate authority. The actual operation and authority determine the filing requirements; a furniture or appliance delivery business is not automatically classified as a household goods carrier.Is BMC-34 the same as cargo insurance?No. The cargo policy provides the coverage, subject to its terms. The BMC-34 is the filing that provides proof of that qualifying coverage to FMCSA.Who files the BMC-34 with FMCSA?The insurance company or its authorized electronic filer submits the filing. Motive can help coordinate the insurance side of the process.What insurance does an interstate moving company need?An interstate moving company may need commercial auto and public liability, motor truck cargo, general liability, workers’ compensation, physical damage, umbrella or excess liability, and property or storage coverage. Required filings and the appropriate coverage depend on the operation.What is the difference between BMC-34 and a public liability filing?BMC-34 provides proof of cargo liability insurance. A public liability filing addresses bodily injury and property damage financial responsibility for commercial vehicle operations. A qualifying carrier may need both.Can Motive help with BMC-34 filing support?Yes. Motive helps review the insurance needs of household goods moving operations and coordinate applicable filing support with the insurer or authorized filer. Start with a quote request or contact our team to discuss your authority and current coverage.Filing references: FMCSA insurance filing requirements and FMCSA registration forms. Coverage is subject to policy terms, conditions, exclusions, and underwriting. The appropriate coverage and filings depend on your operation. FAQsMoving Company Insurance Questions What types of insurance does a household goods moving company typically need? A moving company may need commercial auto liability, physical damage, cargo coverage, general liability, and workers' compensation, depending on its vehicles, employees, contracts, and operations.Motive can help moving companies review the risks associated with transporting customers' furniture and personal property, including loading, delivery, and storage exposures. Does commercial auto insurance protect a customer's furniture and personal belongings during a move? Not automatically. Commercial auto liability primarily addresses covered injury and property damage claims associated with vehicle operations. A moving company may need separate cargo or other specialized protection for customers' belongings.Motive helps movers review the type of property they transport and the relevant insurance terms, rather than assuming a commercial auto policy protects everything inside the truck. What is the difference between cargo insurance and general liability for moving companies? Cargo insurance may protect eligible customer property while it is being transported, subject to policy conditions. General liability addresses certain third-party injury and property damage claims arising from business activities.For example, damaging a customer's property while moving furniture and losing goods during transportation may involve different coverage questions. Motive can help explain these distinctions and identify exclusions that require closer attention. What insurance should a new moving company review before accepting its first customer? Before your first move, review your commercial vehicle coverage, customer-property exposures, general liability needs, employee coverage, and any applicable licensing or transportation requirements.Motive can evaluate your planned moving services, vehicle size, number of employees, and local or interstate operations so you can discuss appropriate insurance before taking possession of a customer's belongings. acceptedAnswer.text: A BMC-34 is proof of cargo liability insurance filed with FMCSA for qualifying household goods motor carriers. It connects the required cargo coverage to the carrier’s federal insurance record.

mainEntity.name: What is a BMC-34 filing?

acceptedAnswer.text: It is relevant to household goods motor carriers operating under applicable interstate authority. The actual operation and authority determine the filing requirements; a furniture or appliance delivery business is not automatically classified as a household goods carrier.

mainEntity.name: Who needs a BMC-34 filing?

acceptedAnswer.text: No. The cargo policy provides the coverage, subject to its terms. The BMC-34 is the filing that provides proof of that qualifying coverage to FMCSA.

mainEntity.name: Is BMC-34 the same as cargo insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: The insurance company or its authorized electronic filer submits the filing. Motive can help coordinate the insurance side of the process.

mainEntity.name: Who files the BMC-34 with FMCSA?

acceptedAnswer.text: An interstate moving company may need commercial auto and public liability, motor truck cargo, general liability, workers’ compensation, physical damage, umbrella or excess liability, and property or storage coverage. Required filings and the appropriate coverage depend on the operation.

mainEntity.name: What insurance does an interstate moving company need?

acceptedAnswer.text: BMC-34 provides proof of cargo liability insurance. A public liability filing addresses bodily injury and property damage financial responsibility for commercial vehicle operations. A qualifying carrier may need both.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between BMC-34 and a public liability filing?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Motive helps review the insurance needs of household goods moving operations and coordinate applicable filing support with the insurer or authorized filer. Start with a quote request or contact our team to discuss your authority and current coverage.

mainEntity.name: Can Motive help with BMC-34 filing support?

acceptedAnswer.text: A moving company may need commercial auto liability, physical damage, cargo coverage, general liability, and workers' compensation, depending on its vehicles, employees, contracts, and operations. Motive can help moving companies review the risks associated with transporting customers' furniture and personal property, including loading, delivery, and storage exposures.

mainEntity.name: What types of insurance does a household goods moving company typically need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not automatically. Commercial auto liability primarily addresses covered injury and property damage claims associated with vehicle operations. A moving company may need separate cargo or other specialized protection for customers' belongings. Motive helps movers review the type of property they transport and the relevant insurance terms, rather than assuming a commercial auto policy protects everything inside the truck.

mainEntity.name: Does commercial auto insurance protect a customer's furniture and personal belongings during a move?

acceptedAnswer.text: Cargo insurance may protect eligible customer property while it is being transported, subject to policy conditions. General liability addresses certain third-party injury and property damage claims arising from business activities. For example, damaging a customer's property while moving furniture and losing goods during transportation may involve different coverage questions. Motive can help explain these distinctions and identify exclusions that require closer attention.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between cargo insurance and general liability for moving companies?

acceptedAnswer.text: Before your first move, review your commercial vehicle coverage, customer-property exposures, general liability needs, employee coverage, and any applicable licensing or transportation requirements. Motive can evaluate your planned moving services, vehicle size, number of employees, and local or interstate operations so you can discuss appropriate insurance before taking possession of a customer's belongings.

mainEntity.name: What insurance should a new moving company review before accepting its first customer?

acceptedAnswer.text: Moving companies should examine how their policies respond to property damage during packing, handling, loading, unloading, and storage. Coverage can differ significantly depending on the activity and whether the goods are in transit or stored at a location. Motive can help businesses ask the right questions about cargo exclusions, property in their care, and any additional protection needed for their services.

mainEntity.name: What additional coverage should movers consider for packing, loading, unloading, and temporary storage?

acceptedAnswer.text: Interstate household goods movers are subject to federal transportation requirements that may differ from those applicable to local movers. Interstate movers also have specific customer-property liability responsibilities. Motive can help review your insurance requirements alongside your planned operating territory and available carrier options. Business owners should separately verify applicable FMCSA and state requirements before expanding across state lines.

MOVING COMPANY INSURANCE · BMC-34 SUPPORT
Household Goods Motor Carrier Insurance

Coverage and BMC-34 filings for moving companies that transport household goods.

Moving household goods creates a different insurance responsibility than simply operating a commercial vehicle. Motive helps household goods motor carriers understand the coverage and filings required around the way they operate.

Commercial auto. Cargo. Liability. BMC-34 filings. One insurance conversation.

Get a Household Goods Insurance Quote
Ask About a BMC-34 Filing →
For the truck, the cargo, and every move.
Commercial auto
Household goods cargo
Business liability
BMC-34 filing support
BUILT AROUND YOUR OPERATION
What is a Household Goods Motor Carrier?

A Household Goods Motor Carrier is a for-hire moving company that transports household goods for the public.

For interstate operations, household goods motor carriers have insurance and operating authority requirements that differ from many other commercial transportation businesses.

More than getting from A to B.
Packing and unpacking
Loading and unloading
Inventorying household goods
Binding or nonbinding estimates
Transportation between homes or other eligible locations
PROTECT EVERY PART OF THE MOVE
Insurance Built for Moving Companies

Your business may be responsible for the truck, the driver, the crew, and your customer’s property. The right insurance program starts with the way you work.

Commercial Auto

Coverage for covered bodily injury, property damage and vehicle exposures involving your moving trucks and vans.

Motor Truck Cargo

Coverage for covered loss or damage to customers’ household goods while your business transports them.

Public Liability

Bodily injury and property damage liability protection arising from commercial vehicle operations.

General Liability

Protection for certain third-party claims from business operations outside the normal auto exposure.

Workers’ Compensation

Coverage related to employee injuries, including the physically demanding work of moving crews.

Physical Damage

Protection for insured vehicles against covered collision and comprehensive losses.

Umbrella or Excess Liability

Additional liability protection above certain underlying policies, when appropriate.

Property or Storage Exposure

Coverage to review when your business has a warehouse or stores customers’ property.

COVERAGE → FILING → FEDERAL RECORD
What Is a BMC-34 Filing?

A BMC-34 is proof of cargo liability insurance filed with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration for qualifying household goods motor carriers.

01 / THE COVERAGE
Cargo Policy

The actual insurance coverage for covered household goods cargo losses.

02 / THE PROOF
BMC-34

Proof of qualifying cargo coverage, submitted by the insurer or authorized electronic filer.

03 / THE RECORD
FMCSA

The filing becomes part of the carrier’s federal insurance and operating authority record.

A BMC-34 is not a separate insurance policy. It is the filing that shows the required cargo liability insurance is in place. Motive can help coordinate the insurance side of that process.

Ask About a BMC-34 Filing →
THE CONNECTION TO YOUR AUTHORITY
Why Does the BMC-34 Matter?

Qualifying interstate household goods carriers need proof of cargo insurance on file with FMCSA. Missing required insurance filings can affect obtaining or maintaining operating authority.

That makes the filing more than paperwork. It connects the policy to your federal insurance record.

Three details to confirm
POLICY
Required cargo coverage is in place
FILING
The insurer has submitted the applicable filing
AUTHORITY
FMCSA’s record reflects the required proof
SEE THE WHOLE INSURANCE PICTURE
BMC-34 Is Only One Part of the Insurance Picture

The filing addresses proof of cargo liability insurance. It does not replace the other coverage your moving business may need.

Coverage and filing responsibilities for a moving-company insurance review
Coverage to review	What it addresses	BMC-34 connection
Motor truck cargo	Customers’ household goods in transit	Proof of qualifying cargo coverage
Commercial auto / public liability	Commercial vehicle liability exposures	Separate liability filing where applicable
General liability	Certain third-party business liability claims	Not established by BMC-34
Workers’ compensation	Employee injuries	Not established by BMC-34
Physical damage	Covered loss to insured vehicles	Not established by BMC-34
Umbrella / excess	Additional liability limits over underlying policies	Not established by BMC-34
Storage / property	Warehouse and stored-property exposures	Separate coverage review needed
DIFFERENT PROOF. DIFFERENT RESPONSIBILITY.
BMC-34 vs. Public Liability Filing
BMC-34
Cargo liability insurance
Household goods cargo exposure
Federal cargo insurance filing
Public Liability Filing
Bodily injury and property damage financial responsibility
Commercial vehicle liability exposure
Separate federal insurance filing where applicable

A qualifying household goods carrier may have both public liability and cargo filing requirements. Motive helps connect those filings to the insurance program.

START WITH YOUR OPERATING AUTHORITY
Who May Need a BMC-34?

A BMC-34 is particularly relevant to businesses operating as household goods motor carriers under applicable interstate authority.

Not every business delivering furniture or appliances is automatically a household goods motor carrier. Your business model and operating authority matter.

Review My Operation →

PERSONAL BELONGINGS. SPECIALIZED RISKS.
Moving Companies Have Different Risks Than General Freight Carriers

Your crew enters customers’ homes, carries furniture through hallways, uses loading ramps, and handles belongings that may be packed, transported, temporarily stored, and unloaded.

A damage claim can involve more than the truck itself. Your insurance should reflect that reality.

Moving Company Insurance Questions
What types of insurance does a household goods moving company typically need?

A moving company may need commercial auto liability, physical damage, cargo coverage, general liability, and workers' compensation, depending on its vehicles, employees, contracts, and operations.

Motive can help moving companies review the risks associated with transporting customers' furniture and personal property, including loading, delivery, and storage exposures.

Does commercial auto insurance protect a customer's furniture and personal belongings during a move?

Not automatically. Commercial auto liability primarily addresses covered injury and property damage claims associated with vehicle operations. A moving company may need separate cargo or other specialized protection for customers' belongings.

Motive helps movers review the type of property they transport and the relevant insurance terms, rather than assuming a commercial auto policy protects everything inside the truck.

What is the difference between cargo insurance and general liability for moving companies?

Cargo insurance may protect eligible customer property while it is being transported, subject to policy conditions. General liability addresses certain third-party injury and property damage claims arising from business activities.

For example, damaging a customer's property while moving furniture and losing goods during transportation may involve different coverage questions. Motive can help explain these distinctions and identify exclusions that require closer attention.

What insurance should a new moving company review before accepting its first customer?

Before your first move, review your commercial vehicle coverage, customer-property exposures, general liability needs, employee coverage, and any applicable licensing or transportation requirements.

Motive can evaluate your planned moving services, vehicle size, number of employees, and local or interstate operations so you can discuss appropriate insurance before taking possession of a customer's belongings.

What additional coverage should movers consider for packing, loading, unloading, and temporary storage?

Moving companies should examine how their policies respond to property damage during packing, handling, loading, unloading, and storage. Coverage can differ significantly depending on the activity and whether the goods are in transit or stored at a location.

Motive can help businesses ask the right questions about cargo exclusions, property in their care, and any additional protection needed for their services.

How do insurance requirements change when a moving company operates across state lines?

Interstate household goods movers are subject to federal transportation requirements that may differ from those applicable to local movers. Interstate movers also have specific customer-property liability responsibilities.

Motive can help review your insurance requirements alongside your planned operating territory and available carrier options. Business owners should separately verify applicable FMCSA and state requirements before expanding across state lines.

Customer vehicles. Drivers. Storage. Contracts.One insurance conversation. Review Your Towing CoverageSee Coverage Areas ↓ Insurance Guide · Updated November 2026 · By Motive Insurance Towing & roadsideProfessional rollback / tow truck operationImage slot — approved towing photograph pending. The whole operationTowing Creates More Than One Insurance RiskA towing company does more than operate a commercial truck.Your business may pick up disabled vehicles, transport customer vehicles, perform roadside assistance, recover damaged vehicles, store vehicles, work with motor clubs, or participate in police and municipal towing programs.Each part of that operation creates a different exposure. That is why tow truck insurance should be reviewed around what your business actually does—not simply the vehicle you drive. Approved photograph requiredRollback tow truck transporting a customer vehicle Car Hauling or Towing — What's the Difference? You may hear the terms car hauling, vehicle transport, and towing used to describe similar types of work. Most customers simply call it towing. Towing & Roadside Insurance

Tow Truck Insurance in Illinois

Insurance built around the real risks of towing, roadside assistance, vehicle recovery, and customer vehicle storage.

Tow trucks. Customer vehicles. Drivers. Storage. Contracts.
One insurance conversation.

Review Your Towing CoverageSee Coverage Areas  ↓

Insurance Guide · Updated November 2026 · By Motive Insurance

Towing & roadside

Professional rollback / tow truck operation

Image slot — approved towing photograph pending.

The whole operation

Towing Creates More Than One Insurance Risk

A towing company does more than operate a commercial truck.

Your business may pick up disabled vehicles, transport customer vehicles, perform roadside assistance, recover damaged vehicles, store vehicles, work with motor clubs, or participate in police and municipal towing programs.

Each part of that operation creates a different exposure. That is why tow truck insurance should be reviewed around what your business actually does—not simply the vehicle you drive.

Approved photograph required

Rollback tow truck transporting a customer vehicle

Car Hauling or Towing — What's the Difference?

You may hear the terms car hauling, vehicle transport, and towing used to describe similar types of work.

Most customers simply call it towing. In the insurance industry, car hauling or vehicle transportation may also be used when describing businesses that move customer vehicles.

Whether you operate a tow truck, rollback, flatbed, or vehicle transporter, the important question is how your business handles the customer's vehicle—and what coverage applies while that vehicle is being transported or stored.

Coverage areas

What Insurance Should a Towing Business Review?

The appropriate coverage depends on your trucks, drivers, services, operating area, customer vehicles, storage operations, and contracts.

Commercial Auto Liability

Commercial auto liability can address covered bodily injury or property damage claims arising from operation of insured commercial vehicles.

Physical Damage

Physical damage can help protect an insured tow truck, rollback, or wrecker against covered collision and comprehensive losses, subject to policy terms and deductibles.

On-Hook Coverage

On-hook coverage is designed to address covered damage to a customer's vehicle while it is being towed or transported by the towing operation.

Garagekeepers Coverage

Garagekeepers coverage addresses customer vehicles being stored or kept in the towing company's care at its location, subject to policy terms.

General Liability

General liability can address certain covered third-party bodily injury or property damage exposures arising from business activities outside normal vehicle operation.

Workers' Compensation

Workers' compensation should be reviewed based on employees, business structure, job duties, and applicable requirements.

Follow the vehicle

Where Is the Customer's Vehicle?

One of the easiest ways to understand towing insurance is to follow the customer's vehicle through the operation.
