Customer vehicle is stored at your location

Garagekeepers Coverage

The tow truck and the customer's vehicle are not the same insurance exposure.

A towing company that transports vehicles and stores them should review both parts of that risk.

Illinois registration

Illinois Tow Truck Insurance Requirements

Illinois establishes minimum insurance requirements for tow-truck registration.

Illinois tow-truck registration insurance minimums
Coverage	Illinois Registration Minimum
Automobile Liability	$500,000 CSL
Garage Liability	$500,000 CSL
On-Hook Coverage	$25,000
Garagekeepers Coverage	$25,000
Workers' Compensation	When applicable

CSL means combined single limit. Source: Illinois Secretary of State tow-truck registration guidance (PDF).

Certain exceptions can apply depending on the operation. These amounts are registration minimums—not necessarily the amount of insurance every towing company should carry.

Illinois minimums do not automatically equal your contract requirements or your actual business exposure.

2026 Illinois Update

Illinois strengthened portions of its commercial towing enforcement framework in 2026. Towing companies should verify the current registration, Illinois Commerce Commission, local, contractual, and insurance requirements that apply to their specific operation.

Read the Illinois State Police legislative update (PDF, page 45)
On-Hook vs. Garagekeepers: What's the Difference?

On-Hook

Customer vehicle is being:
Loaded
Towed
Carried
Transported

Think: the customer's vehicle is moving with you.

Garagekeepers

Customer vehicle is:
Stored
Held
Parked at the towing facility
In the company's care at its location

Think: the customer's vehicle is staying with you.

Transporting → Review on-hookStoring → Review garagekeepers

If your business does both, your insurance review should address both exposures.

Loading, unloading and storage protection depend on the policy wording, limits and exclusions. Confirm when each coverage applies.

Before you sign

Minimum Coverage May Not Satisfy Every Towing Contract

A towing company can meet a state registration requirement and still need higher insurance limits for certain work.

Police rotation programs
Municipalities
Motor clubs
Auto dealerships
Repair facilities
Commercial fleets
Property managers
Government agencies

Some towing arrangements can require insurance limits above the basic tow-truck registration minimums.

Before signing a towing contract, review its insurance requirements, including applicable liability limits, on-hook limits, garagekeepers requirements, general liability, workers' compensation, certificates of insurance, and additional insured requirements.

The legal minimum is not always the contractual minimum.

What Type of Towing Operation Do You Run?

Insurance should reflect the work you actually perform.

Light-Duty Towing
Rollback & Flatbed Towing
Wrecker & Wheel-Lift Operations
Roadside Assistance
Vehicle Recovery
Storage & Impound
Police & Municipal Rotation
Towing Fleets

Prepare for a useful conversation

Preparing for a Towing Insurance Review

Accurate information helps match the insurance conversation to the operation you actually run.

Tow trucks and VINs
Truck types and values
Drivers
Towing radius
Types of towing performed
Roadside assistance services
Vehicle recovery work
Customer vehicle storage
Police or municipal rotation work
Motor-club or commercial contracts
Current on-hook limits
Current garagekeepers limits
Prior claims or loss runs
Current insurance
Renewal date
Review Your Towing Coverage

Towing insurance questions

Frequently Asked Questions
What insurance does a towing company need in Illinois?

Illinois towing businesses may need commercial auto liability, on-hook, garagekeepers, garage liability, and workers' compensation when applicable. Exact requirements depend on the operation and contracts.

What is on-hook towing insurance?

On-hook coverage helps protect a customer's vehicle while it is being towed or transported. Coverage depends on the policy's limits, terms, deductible, and exclusions.

What is the difference between on-hook and garagekeepers insurance?

On-hook generally applies while a customer's vehicle is being transported. Garagekeepers addresses customer vehicles being stored or kept in your care at your location.

How much insurance does an Illinois tow truck need?

Illinois establishes minimum insurance requirements for tow-truck registration, but contracts and certain towing programs may require higher limits. Your limits should reflect both applicable requirements and how your business operates.

Can a new towing company get insurance?

Yes, new towing businesses may qualify. Insurers typically review the trucks, drivers, towing services, operating radius, storage operations, driving history, and requested coverage.

Your trucks are only one part of the risk.

raw.text: Black Car & Limousine InsuranceA guide to vehicle values, passengers, chauffeurs, contracts, and insurance considerations in executive and private transportation. Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive InsuranceWhen clients hire an executive transportation company, they expect professionalism from pickup to destination.Your insurance should be approached with the same level of attention.This guide explains coverage considerations for black car, limousine, chauffeur, and executive transportation businesses, including vehicle values, passengers, drivers, and contracts.Who needs black car insurance?Black car insurance may apply to businesses providing: Executive transportationCorporate transportationLimousine servicesChauffeur servicesPrivate car servicesAirport transportationVIP transportationEvent transportationHourly transportationPrearranged passenger service The specific insurance needs depend on how the company operates. A single owner-driven luxury sedan is not the same risk as a fleet of SUVs and limousines serving corporate accounts.Commercial auto for black car operationsPersonal auto insurance is generally not designed for vehicles being used as part of a commercial passenger transportation business. Commercial auto coverage should reflect the vehicle's business use. Underwriters may examine: Vehicle typeVehicle valuePassenger capacityDriver historyOperating areaAnnual mileageAirport activityYears in businessContractsClaims history The details matter. A luxury SUV used for executive transportation presents a different insurance profile from an ordinary passenger vehicle used for personal commuting.Passenger exposureExecutive transportation companies are responsible for people. That passenger exposure should be part of the insurance conversation from the beginning. Passenger volume, vehicle capacity, interstate trips and the structure of the operation can affect applicable insurance requirements and underwriting.Limousine insuranceLimousines can create additional insurance considerations because of: Vehicle configurationPassenger capacityVehicle valueSpecialty equipmentOperating hoursEvent transportationAlcohol-related exposuresDriver requirementsLong-distance trips These factors should be disclosed accurately when requesting limousine insurance. An insurance comparison is not meaningful if the business use, vehicles, or passenger responsibilities have been described incorrectly.Airport and corporate transportationMany black car companies build their business around airports and corporate clients. That can mean: Frequent airport tripsAdvance reservationsCorporate agreementsHotel partnershipsTravel-management relationshipsHigh annual mileageMultiple driversLate-night or early-morning operations Insurance should evolve with those contracts. A company that began with one vehicle and private clients may need a different structure once it begins servicing larger commercial accounts.Physical damage for high-value vehiclesExecutive transportation fleets frequently use late-model SUVs, sedans and specialty vehicles. Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles from covered collision and comprehensive losses. Vehicle valuation and deductible choices deserve particular attention when the fleet includes high-value vehicles.General liability and business exposureYour risk does not always begin and end inside the vehicle. Umbrella or excess liability can provide additional limits above certain underlying policies when appropriate and available.What affects black car insurance cost?Insurance carriers may review: Number of vehiclesLuxury vehicle valuesVehicle agePassenger capacityDriver age and experienceMotor vehicle recordsClaims historyOperating radiusAirport useAnnual mileageHours of operationCorporate contractsInterstate travelRequested limitsDeductiblesFrom one black car to a transportation fleetGrowth changes the insurance problem. One vehicle becomes three. Three becomes ten. Then the business adds drivers, contracts, dispatching, certificates, new vehicles and new service areas. Insurance should be reviewed at each stage. Review the operation as a transportation business rather than treating each vehicle as an unrelated policy decision.Insurance that matches the serviceYour clients expect a professional driver. A professional vehicle. A professional experience. Your insurance program should receive the same consideration. mainEntity.name: What is black car insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Black car insurance generally refers to commercial insurance for businesses providing prearranged private passenger transportation using sedans, SUVs or other vehicles.

mainEntity.name: Do limousine companies need commercial auto insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: A limousine used commercially should be evaluated for appropriate commercial insurance based on its business use, passenger capacity, vehicle configuration and applicable requirements.

mainEntity.name: Does black car insurance cover the vehicle?

acceptedAnswer.text: Physical damage coverage may be purchased to help protect an insured vehicle against covered collision and comprehensive losses, subject to the policy.

mainEntity.name: What changes when a black car business becomes a fleet?

acceptedAnswer.text: Additional vehicles can introduce different values, drivers, seating capacities, service areas, and contracts. Update the vehicle and driver schedules and identify any changes in how the business accepts or fulfills trips.

mainEntity.name: Why is passenger capacity important?

acceptedAnswer.text: Passenger capacity can influence underwriting and, for certain interstate for-hire passenger operations, applicable financial responsibility requirements.

Specialty Transportation
Black Car & Limousine Insurance
Black Car & Limousine Insurance

A guide to vehicle values, passengers, chauffeurs, contracts, and insurance considerations in executive and private transportation.

Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance

When clients hire an executive transportation company, they expect professionalism from pickup to destination.

Your insurance should be approached with the same level of attention.

This guide explains coverage considerations for black car, limousine, chauffeur, and executive transportation businesses, including vehicle values, passengers, drivers, and contracts.

Who needs black car insurance?

Black car insurance may apply to businesses providing:

Executive transportation
Corporate transportation
Limousine services
Chauffeur services
Private car services
Airport transportation
VIP transportation
Event transportation
Hourly transportation
Prearranged passenger service

The specific insurance needs depend on how the company operates.

A single owner-driven luxury sedan is not the same risk as a fleet of SUVs and limousines serving corporate accounts.

Commercial auto for black car operations

Personal auto insurance is generally not designed for vehicles being used as part of a commercial passenger transportation business.

Commercial auto coverage should reflect the vehicle's business use.

Underwriters may examine:

Vehicle type
Vehicle value
Passenger capacity
Driver history
Operating area
Annual mileage
Airport activity
Years in business
Contracts
Claims history

The details matter.

A luxury SUV used for executive transportation presents a different insurance profile from an ordinary passenger vehicle used for personal commuting.

Passenger exposure

Executive transportation companies are responsible for people.

That passenger exposure should be part of the insurance conversation from the beginning.

Passenger volume, vehicle capacity, interstate trips and the structure of the operation can affect applicable insurance requirements and underwriting.

Limousine insurance

Limousines can create additional insurance considerations because of:

Vehicle configuration
Passenger capacity
Vehicle value
Specialty equipment
Operating hours
Event transportation
Alcohol-related exposures
Driver requirements
Long-distance trips

These factors should be disclosed accurately when requesting limousine insurance.

An insurance comparison is not meaningful if the business use, vehicles, or passenger responsibilities have been described incorrectly.

Airport and corporate transportation

Many black car companies build their business around airports and corporate clients.

That can mean:

Frequent airport trips
Advance reservations
Corporate agreements
Hotel partnerships
Travel-management relationships
High annual mileage
Multiple drivers
Late-night or early-morning operations

Insurance should evolve with those contracts.

A company that began with one vehicle and private clients may need a different structure once it begins servicing larger commercial accounts.

Physical damage for high-value vehicles

Executive transportation fleets frequently use late-model SUVs, sedans and specialty vehicles.

Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles from covered collision and comprehensive losses.

Vehicle valuation and deductible choices deserve particular attention when the fleet includes high-value vehicles.

General liability and business exposure

Your risk does not always begin and end inside the vehicle.

General liability may be relevant for certain third-party claims connected to business operations outside normal automobile liability.

Workers' compensation

A company employing chauffeurs, dispatchers or other staff should also review workers' compensation requirements and employee exposures.

Umbrella and excess liability

Executive transportation companies may work with clients or contracts requiring higher liability limits.

Umbrella or excess liability can provide additional limits above certain underlying policies when appropriate and available.

What affects black car insurance cost?

Insurance carriers may review:

Number of vehicles
Luxury vehicle values
Vehicle age
Passenger capacity
Driver age and experience
Motor vehicle records
Claims history
Operating radius
Airport use
Annual mileage
Hours of operation
Corporate contracts
Interstate travel
Requested limits
Deductibles
From one black car to a transportation fleet

Growth changes the insurance problem.

One vehicle becomes three.

Three becomes ten.

Then the business adds drivers, contracts, dispatching, certificates, new vehicles and new service areas.

Insurance should be reviewed at each stage.

Review the operation as a transportation business rather than treating each vehicle as an unrelated policy decision.

Insurance that matches the service

Your clients expect a professional driver.

A professional vehicle.

A professional experience.

Your insurance program should receive the same consideration.

The most useful review follows the service from reservation and pickup through the completed trip.

Coverage comparison
Black car and limousine coverage review points
Situation	Review area	Question to ask
Commercial passenger use	Business use of the vehicle	Does the policy description match prearranged passenger transportation?
High-value SUV or sedan	Physical damage valuation	Which valuation method, deductible, and equipment details apply?
Limousine configuration	Capacity and modifications	Are the seating arrangement and specialty equipment accurately scheduled?
Corporate or airport agreement	Contractual responsibilities	What limits, documentation, or endorsements are requested?
Added chauffeurs or vehicles	Fleet and driver schedules	Have the new drivers, vehicles, values, and service areas been reviewed?
A practical example
Example: replacing a sedan with a higher-value SUV

A chauffeur business replaces a sedan with a newer luxury SUV for corporate trips. Compare more than the model year: review the purchase value, seating capacity, equipment, deductible, and valuation wording. Update vehicle records and any certificates affected by the change. A vehicle substitution is an opportunity to check the service description, not proof that every difference is automatically insured.

Common mistakes to avoid
Assuming a personal policy matches commercial passenger use

Identify how trips are booked and how the vehicle is used. A vehicle’s appearance does not determine whether its insurance description fits the business activity.

Leaving valuation questions until after a loss

Purchase price, loan balance, and a policy’s loss-settlement method are different concepts. Read the applicable wording before assuming the amounts are interchangeable.

Keeping an outdated driver list

A growing operation can use several chauffeurs across different vehicles. Keep current records of who drives, where, and under which business arrangement.

Your document review checklist

Use these prompts to organize your documents and identify unanswered questions. Completing the list does not confirm coverage.

Mark the items you have reviewed
Commercial passenger use described accuratelyVehicle values and equipment documentedSeating configurations recordedChauffeur arrangements and driver records currentCorporate and airport contracts reviewed
0 of 5 items reviewed
Frequently asked questions
What is black car insurance?
Do limousine companies need commercial auto insurance?
Does black car insurance cover the vehicle?
What changes when a black car business becomes a fleet?
Why is passenger capacity important?
Sources and further reading

Certain interstate passenger operations fall within FMCSA insurance requirements. Check the actual service, vehicle configuration, and applicable exceptions rather than applying one rule to every private-car business.

FMCSA: insurance filing requirements
NAIC: small business insurance

This guide explains general insurance considerations. Policy wording, exclusions, state requirements, and the facts of an operation determine what applies.

mainEntity.name: What insurance does a car hauler need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Depending on the operation, a car hauler may need commercial auto liability, motor truck cargo, physical damage, general liability, workers' compensation and additional coverage.

mainEntity.name: Does cargo insurance cover cars being transported?

acceptedAnswer.text: Motor truck cargo insurance may provide coverage for customer vehicles being transported, subject to the policy's terms, conditions, limits, deductibles and exclusions.

mainEntity.name: How much cargo insurance does a car hauler need?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single appropriate limit for every operation. Consider the maximum number of vehicles hauled and the maximum combined value that could be on one load.

mainEntity.name: Does enclosed auto transport require different insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: The fundamental coverage categories may be similar, but enclosed carriers frequently transport higher-value vehicles. Vehicle values and maximum cargo exposure should be discussed with the insurer.

mainEntity.name: What should a new car hauling business review first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the truck, trailer, expected loads, customer contracts, operating area, and driver experience. Work out the maximum total vehicle value on one load and ask how the policy addresses loading, unloading, storage, and exclusions.

mainEntity.name: What insurance does a car hauler need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Depending on the operation, a car hauler may need commercial auto liability, motor truck cargo, physical damage, general liability, workers' compensation and additional coverage.

mainEntity.name: Does cargo insurance cover cars being transported?

acceptedAnswer.text: Motor truck cargo insurance may provide coverage for customer vehicles being transported, subject to the policy's terms, conditions, limits, deductibles and exclusions.

mainEntity.name: How much cargo insurance does a car hauler need?

acceptedAnswer.text: There is no single appropriate limit for every operation. Consider the maximum number of vehicles hauled and the maximum combined value that could be on one load.

mainEntity.name: Does enclosed auto transport require different insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: The fundamental coverage categories may be similar, but enclosed carriers frequently transport higher-value vehicles. Vehicle values and maximum cargo exposure should be discussed with the insurer.

mainEntity.name: What should a new car hauling business review first?

acceptedAnswer.text: Start with the truck, trailer, expected loads, customer contracts, operating area, and driver experience. Work out the maximum total vehicle value on one load and ask how the policy addresses loading, unloading, storage, and exclusions.

Car Hauling Insurance
Car Hauling Insurance

A guide to auto transport insurance questions, from truck and trailer protection to customer vehicle values and pickup-to-delivery responsibilities.

Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance

When you haul a vehicle, you are responsible for more than your truck and trailer.

You are also responsible for somebody else's automobile.

One load may represent tens or hundreds of thousands of dollars in customer property.

This guide explains the differences between commercial auto, cargo, equipment, and business liability considerations for vehicle transport operations.

What is car hauling insurance?

Car hauling insurance is commercial insurance structured around businesses transporting automobiles and other vehicles.

Operations may include:

Single-car hauling
Multi-car hauling
Auto transport
Dealer vehicle transport
Auction transport
Vehicle relocation
Enclosed vehicle transport
Open vehicle transport
Classic car transport
Luxury vehicle transport
Fleet vehicle relocation
Interstate auto transport

Each operation should be evaluated based on what is being transported and how.

Commercial auto liability

The power unit is still a commercial vehicle.

Commercial auto liability can help address covered bodily injury and property damage resulting from the operation of insured commercial vehicles.

The truck, trailer, driver, routes and operating radius should all be represented accurately.

Motor truck cargo for vehicle transporters

Cargo coverage is a major consideration for car haulers because the cargo is the customer's vehicle.

The value of a load can increase quickly.

Consider a trailer carrying:

Several late-model vehicles
Luxury vehicles
Classic automobiles
Dealer inventory
Specialty vehicles

A cargo limit that appears adequate for one type of load may be insufficient for another.

Car haulers should evaluate:

Maximum number of vehicles per load
Average vehicle value
Maximum vehicle value
Maximum total load value
Open versus enclosed transport
Loading procedures
Securement
Storage
Routes
Deductibles
Cargo exclusions

The cargo limit should reflect real operations—not an arbitrary number chosen only to satisfy a certificate requirement.

Physical damage for the truck and trailer

Cargo coverage protects a different interest than physical damage coverage.

Physical damage can help protect insured trucks and trailers against covered collision and comprehensive losses.

A complete review should consider the value of:

Power unit
Trailer
Specialized equipment
Aftermarket additions
Loading and unloading exposure

Car hauling risk does not begin once the truck reaches highway speed.

Damage can happen while a vehicle is:

Driven onto the trailer
Positioned
Secured
Moved between decks
Unloaded
Transferred
Stored temporarily

Loading procedures, driver experience and equipment condition all matter.

Open vs. enclosed car hauling

Open car carriers and enclosed transporters can have different exposures.

Enclosed transport is often used for:

Luxury automobiles
Classic vehicles
Exotic vehicles
Collector cars
Specialty vehicles

Higher individual vehicle values should be discussed with the insurer.

Do not assume a standard cargo limit automatically matches a high-value auto transport operation.

Dealer and auction vehicle transport

Car haulers may move vehicles for:

Auto dealerships
Dealer groups
Auto auctions
Fleet operators
Rental companies
Manufacturers
Private customers

Commercial contracts may establish their own insurance requirements.

Compare requested limits and certificates with the actual loads, contracts, and policy wording.

General liability

Some vehicle transport businesses also have premises, loading areas or other operations outside normal highway transportation.

General liability may help address certain covered third-party business claims not arising from auto liability.

Workers' compensation

Drivers and employees may be injured while loading, securing, inspecting or transporting vehicles.

Workers' compensation should be considered based on staffing and applicable state requirements.

Umbrella or excess liability

Larger auto transport operations and certain contracts may require higher liability limits.

Umbrella or excess liability may be appropriate depending on the underlying coverage and business requirements.

Documents for a car hauling insurance review

Organize the following information before comparing coverage:

Number of trucks
Number of trailers
Truck values
Trailer values
Driver information
USDOT information when applicable
Operating radius
States of operation
Types of vehicles transported
Maximum vehicle value
Maximum load value
Average number of vehicles per load
Open or enclosed transport
Customers and contracts
Annual mileage
Loss history
Current insurance
Requested cargo limit
Renewal date
What affects car hauling insurance cost?

Insurance carriers may consider:

Equipment
Drivers
Operating history
Radius
Claims
Cargo values
Vehicle types transported
Trailer configuration
Number of vehicles hauled
Contracts
Annual mileage
Coverage limits
Deductibles
Starting a car hauling business?

Do not build the business first and ask about insurance at the last minute.

Before accepting your first transport job, understand:

What truck you will operate
What trailer you will use
What vehicles you will transport
Where you will operate
How much cargo value you may carry
What contracts require
Which filings or authority may apply to your operation
What information insurers will request

Insurance is part of the operating model.

Resolve the insurance questions alongside equipment, operating authority, and contract planning before accepting a transport assignment.

From one trailer to a car-hauling fleet

Growth creates new complexity.

Additional trucks mean additional drivers.

Additional trailers mean additional values.

Larger contracts can increase cargo concentration.

Longer routes increase mileage.

Higher-end clients can increase vehicle values.

A growing car hauling business should review insurance as those variables change.

Protect the equipment and the vehicles you are paid to move

The truck matters.

The trailer matters.

The driver matters.

The customer's vehicle matters.

Car hauling insurance should account for all four.

Compare coverage against the actual equipment, routes, vehicle values, and responsibilities in the operation.

Coverage comparison
Separate the equipment from the customer vehicles
Situation	Review area	Question to ask
Power unit in a road accident	Commercial auto liability	Which insured vehicles and transportation activities are described?
Damage to your truck or trailer	Physical damage	How are equipment values, deductibles, and modifications addressed?
Damage to customer vehicles	Motor truck cargo or applicable transit coverage	What property, activities, limits, exclusions, and valuation wording apply?
Loading, unloading, or a transfer	The applicable policy wording	When does coverage attach and end, and which handling activities are included?
A dealer or auction agreement	Contract and insurance documentation	Do requested limits and obligations match the loads and policy terms?
A practical example
Example: calculate the total value on one load

For illustration, six customer vehicles valued at $40,000 each create $240,000 in combined vehicle value. That arithmetic is a starting point for a cargo-limit discussion, not a recommended limit or a promise of payment. Check any per-vehicle restrictions, valuation terms, deductibles, exclusions, and maximum exposure on other loads. A load with fewer luxury vehicles can be worth more than a full load of lower-value vehicles.

Common mistakes to avoid
Confusing a filing requirement with cargo protection

Regulatory filings and protection for customer vehicles answer different questions. Review the applicable rules alongside the cargo policy and customer contracts.

Using an average load instead of a maximum load

Track the highest reasonably expected combined vehicle value and any concentration of expensive vehicles. Revisit that figure when accepting new customers or equipment.

Assuming loading and temporary storage are automatically included

Read when coverage begins and ends. Identify who loads, unloads, transfers, or stores vehicles and ask how each activity is treated.

Your document review checklist

Use these prompts to organize your documents and identify unanswered questions. Completing the list does not confirm coverage.

Mark the items you have reviewed
Truck, trailer, and equipment values recordedMaximum individual and combined vehicle values calculatedOpen or enclosed operations documentedLoading, unloading, and custody responsibilities identifiedContracts and cargo terms compared
0 of 5 items reviewed
Frequently asked questions
What insurance does a car hauler need?
Does cargo insurance cover cars being transported?
How much cargo insurance does a car hauler need?
Does enclosed auto transport require different insurance?
What should a new car hauling business review first?
Sources and further reading

FMCSA distinguishes its cargo-filing requirements for household-goods operations from other carrier categories. Do not assume that a federal filing rule establishes adequate protection for an auto transporter’s customer vehicles.

raw.description: Compare commercial fleet insurance coverage, cost factors, and quote requirements for trucks, vans, and mixed business fleets with Motive Insurance.
raw.text: A guide for growing businessesCommercialFleet InsuranceMore vehicles. More moving parts.Build a coverage review around the way your business actually runs.Review My Fleet Coverage ↗Call 888-943-0888 The quick answerWhat is commercial fleet insurance?Commercial fleet insurance is an approach to insuring multiple business vehicles through a coordinated commercial auto policy or program. It can simplify renewals and vehicle changes, but the coverage still needs to reflect each vehicle, driver, and business use.There is no single vehicle count that makes every business a fleet. Carrier programs have different eligibility rules. Progressive, for example, distinguishes standard commercial auto, small fleet, and larger or specialized fleet programs. Read Progressive's fleet insurance guide.For your review, start with a practical question: does your current insurance arrangement still fit the number of vehicles you operate and the work they perform? Start with your operationWhich businesses should review fleet coverage?A useful review starts with what happens during a working day. Describe the routes, stops, drivers, and property carried before comparing policy labels. 01Delivery and box truck businessesBring a list of delivery contracts, typical loads, and operating areas. Identify whether you transport your own products or freight belonging to customers.Explore commercial truck insurance → 02Contractors and service teamsList work vans, pickups, trailers, and the tools that travel with each crew. Flag vehicles that stay at employees' homes or serve several job sites.Explore commercial van insurance → 03Businesses with mixed vehiclesSeparate company cars, service vans, and larger trucks on your vehicle list. Explain who uses each one and whether vehicles are owned, leased, or rented.Prepare your vehicle list → Build the coverage pictureWhat does fleet insurance cover?Liability and protection for the vehicle address different losses. Use this comparison to ask what a proposed policy actually includes. Every coverage is subject to its terms, limits, deductibles, and exclusions. Commercial fleet coverage and questions to ask during a reviewCoverage to reviewWhat it may addressAsk before you choose Auto liabilityCovered bodily injury or property damage claims involving others arising from insured vehicle use.Which vehicles and uses qualify, and do the limits meet your contracts? CollisionCovered damage to an insured vehicle from a collision or overturn.What deductible applies to each vehicle? ComprehensiveCovered non-collision losses, such as theft, fire, or vandalism.How is a vehicle valued after a total loss? Uninsured / underinsured motoristCertain losses involving a driver with insufficient insurance, depending on state law and policy terms.What protection is offered or required for your operation? Hired / non-owned auto liabilitySpecified business liability involving rented vehicles or employees' personal vehicles used for work.What separate protection is needed for damage to those vehicles? Coverage reference: Travelers' commercial auto coverage overview. This educational reference does not imply a Motive appointment with that insurer. The vehicle and its contents need separate attentionAdd a second list for freight, tools, equipment, and customer property. Ask the agent to identify the policy or endorsement that would address each item. Do the same for loading, unloading, and storage activities. Write down unresolved questions before accepting the quote. Beyond company-owned vehiclesDo employees ever drive their own cars for work?An employee making a business errand in a personal car can create a liability exposure for the company. Non-owned auto liability may address certain claims involving that activity; it generally does not pay to repair the employee's car.Renting a replacement vehicle raises another question: does your arrangement include hired auto liability and any needed physical damage coverage? Describe both situations during your review, including how often they occur.See Progressive's explanation of non-owned auto coverage. Understand the priceHow much does commercial fleet insurance cost?Your vehicle count alone cannot produce a meaningful estimate. Vehicle types, driving history, business use, garaging locations, limits, and deductibles can affect the price. Fleet arrangements may offer administrative advantages, but savings are not guaranteed.Compare the same coveragePut quotes side by side with matching vehicle and driver lists. Check the liability limit, physical damage deductibles, covered uses, exclusions, and any additional protections. A lower payment deserves a closer look if one quote leaves out a vehicle or coverage you asked to include.Look at the full payment scheduleRecord the total quoted premium, initial payment, installment amounts, and any listed fees. nojs.mainText:
A guide for growing businesses

Commercial
Fleet Insurance

More vehicles. More moving parts.
Build a coverage review around the way your business actually runs.

Review My Fleet Coverage ↗Call 888-943-0888
Home / Commercial Fleet Insurance
Fleet basicsCoverageCost factorsQuote checklistFAQs

The quick answer

What is commercial fleet insurance?

Commercial fleet insurance is an approach to insuring multiple business vehicles through a coordinated commercial auto policy or program. It can simplify renewals and vehicle changes, but the coverage still needs to reflect each vehicle, driver, and business use.

There is no single vehicle count that makes every business a fleet. Carrier programs have different eligibility rules. Progressive, for example, distinguishes standard commercial auto, small fleet, and larger or specialized fleet programs. Read Progressive's fleet insurance guide.

For your review, start with a practical question: does your current insurance arrangement still fit the number of vehicles you operate and the work they perform?

Start with your operation

Which businesses should review fleet coverage?

A useful review starts with what happens during a working day. Describe the routes, stops, drivers, and property carried before comparing policy labels.

01
Delivery and box truck businesses

Bring a list of delivery contracts, typical loads, and operating areas. Identify whether you transport your own products or freight belonging to customers.

Explore commercial truck insurance →
02
Contractors and service teams

List work vans, pickups, trailers, and the tools that travel with each crew. Flag vehicles that stay at employees' homes or serve several job sites.

Explore commercial van insurance →
03
Businesses with mixed vehicles

Separate company cars, service vans, and larger trucks on your vehicle list. Explain who uses each one and whether vehicles are owned, leased, or rented.

Prepare your vehicle list →

Build the coverage picture

What does fleet insurance cover?

Liability and protection for the vehicle address different losses. Use this comparison to ask what a proposed policy actually includes. Every coverage is subject to its terms, limits, deductibles, and exclusions.

Commercial fleet coverage and questions to ask during a review
Coverage to review	What it may address	Ask before you choose
Auto liability	Covered bodily injury or property damage claims involving others arising from insured vehicle use.	Which vehicles and uses qualify, and do the limits meet your contracts?
Collision	Covered damage to an insured vehicle from a collision or overturn.	What deductible applies to each vehicle?
Comprehensive	Covered non-collision losses, such as theft, fire, or vandalism.	How is a vehicle valued after a total loss?
Uninsured / underinsured motorist	Certain losses involving a driver with insufficient insurance, depending on state law and policy terms.	What protection is offered or required for your operation?
Hired / non-owned auto liability	Specified business liability involving rented vehicles or employees' personal vehicles used for work.	What separate protection is needed for damage to those vehicles?

Coverage reference: Travelers' commercial auto coverage overview. This educational reference does not imply a Motive appointment with that insurer.

The vehicle and its contents need separate attention

Add a second list for freight, tools, equipment, and customer property. Ask the agent to identify the policy or endorsement that would address each item. Do the same for loading, unloading, and storage activities. Write down unresolved questions before accepting the quote.

Beyond company-owned vehicles

Do employees ever drive their own cars for work?

An employee making a business errand in a personal car can create a liability exposure for the company. Non-owned auto liability may address certain claims involving that activity; it generally does not pay to repair the employee's car.

Renting a replacement vehicle raises another question: does your arrangement include hired auto liability and any needed physical damage coverage? Describe both situations during your review, including how often they occur.

See Progressive's explanation of non-owned auto coverage.

A practical fleet example

Imagine a service business with four vans, a pickup, and an employee who sometimes uses a personal car to collect supplies.

Its review should account for all three arrangements. Listing the five company vehicles is only the starting point. Bring the personal-car use, equipment carried, and occasional rentals into the same conversation.

Illustrative planning example; coverage depends on the actual policy.

Understand the price

How much does commercial fleet insurance cost?

Your vehicle count alone cannot produce a meaningful estimate. Vehicle types, driving history, business use, garaging locations, limits, and deductibles can affect the price. Fleet arrangements may offer administrative advantages, but savings are not guaranteed.

Compare the same coverage

Put quotes side by side with matching vehicle and driver lists. Check the liability limit, physical damage deductibles, covered uses, exclusions, and any additional protections. A lower payment deserves a closer look if one quote leaves out a vehicle or coverage you asked to include.

Look at the full payment schedule

Record the total quoted premium, initial payment, installment amounts, and any listed fees. Keep the quote date and proposed effective date with the comparison so you can ask about changes before making a decision.

Bring evidence of how you manage the fleet

Prepare your driver-selection process, maintenance records, and any safety or telematics information you already keep. Ask which details the insurer considers and whether any eligible program could affect your quote.

Test the deductible against your budget

Compare the proposed deductibles with the cash your business could make available after a loss. Ask for alternative quotes if you want to understand the premium difference, and document the tradeoff before choosing.

Pricing factors and program considerations: Progressive Commercial and Travelers.

Make the review useful

Your fleet insurance quote checklist

You do not need a polished presentation. A current spreadsheet and your existing policy documents give the conversation a clearer starting point.

Keep an extra column for anything you still need to confirm. Motive can help identify which details are needed for the available options.

01
Business details

Gather the legal business name, address, contact details, description of operations, and current policy renewal date.

02
Vehicle schedule

List each VIN, year, make, model, garaging address, ownership or lease status, and the work it performs. Include trailers for discussion.

03
Driver roster

Prepare the current driver list and assignments. Ask how to provide license details securely and which driving-history information is needed.

04
Routes and loads

Describe typical mileage, operating radius, states traveled, and the goods or equipment carried. Note seasonal changes.

05
Current coverage and claims

Have declarations, endorsements, and available claims information ready. Ask whether the insurer needs formal loss runs.

06
Contracts and planned changes

Collect customer insurance requirements and details of upcoming vehicle purchases, hires, rentals, or new delivery contracts.

Keep records current

Review changes before the next vehicle goes to work

Create a simple handoff between whoever buys vehicles, hires drivers, and manages insurance. Give one person responsibility for reporting changes and retaining the insurer's response.

For each request, record the vehicle or driver involved, the requested effective date, and the confirmation received. Follow the policy's reporting conditions; do not assume a purchase receipt or an emailed request confirms coverage.

At renewal, compare the policy schedule with your actual operation. Flag sold vehicles, new garaging locations, revised routes, and changes in the type of work you accept.

Already a Motive customer? Use our policy-change page to start a request.

Commercial Fleet Insurance
Questions
What is fleet insurance, and how is it different from insuring vehicles individually?

Fleet insurance can allow businesses to insure multiple commercial vehicles under a coordinated policy arrangement rather than maintaining unrelated policies for every vehicle.

For businesses operating delivery trucks, contractor vans, service vehicles, or multiple box trucks, Motive can help review available fleet coverage options, driver requirements, liability limits, and operational risks.

The goal is to simplify coverage management while protecting the vehicles that generate business revenue.

How many vehicles do I need before considering fleet insurance?

You do not necessarily need a large transportation company to begin discussing fleet insurance. Some insurers offer multi-vehicle commercial arrangements for smaller businesses, while dedicated fleet programs may have minimum vehicle or other underwriting requirements.

Motive can assess your number of vehicles, business use, and expansion plans to determine which commercial insurance approach is worth comparing.

Can one fleet policy cover different types of vehicles, including trucks and vans?

Depending on the carrier and business operation, a commercial policy may accommodate different vehicle types, including delivery vans, box trucks, and service vehicles.

However, some specialized trucking risks require separate arrangements. Motive helps business owners review their entire vehicle inventory rather than assuming every commercial vehicle belongs under the same coverage.

What happens to my fleet insurance when I add or remove vehicles or drivers?

Adding or removing a vehicle or driver can change the coverage details and premium of your commercial insurance policy. New vehicles and drivers should be reported according to your insurer's policy conditions before they are placed into service.

Motive can help you request changes and review the updated policy documents so your records reflect the vehicles and drivers used by your business.

How can a business reduce fleet insurance costs without sacrificing important coverage?

Fleet insurance costs may be influenced by driving records, claims experience, vehicle type, safety procedures, deductibles, and how vehicles are used.

Motive helps businesses review these factors, compare eligible insurance options, and identify areas where costs may be managed without automatically lowering important liability or physical damage protection.

raw.text: NEMT InsuranceA practical guide to insurance considerations for medical transportation vehicles, passengers, drivers, accessibility equipment, and contracts. Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive InsuranceNon-emergency medical transportation businesses do more than move passengers from one address to another.Your drivers may transport seniors, Medicaid members, passengers using wheelchairs, people traveling to dialysis or therapy appointments, and individuals who need additional assistance entering or exiting a vehicle.That creates a different risk profile than an ordinary commercial vehicle.This guide explains the coverage categories, operational details, and contract questions that belong in an NEMT insurance review.Commercial auto. Passenger exposure. Wheelchair transportation. Drivers. Contracts. Business liability.One insurance conversation.What is NEMT insurance?NEMT insurance is commercial insurance structured around businesses providing non-emergency medical transportation. It may apply to operations such as: Non-emergency medical transportationWheelchair transportationAmbulette servicesSenior transportationMedicaid transportationDialysis transportationMedical appointment transportationMobility-assisted transportationPrivate-pay medical transportation The appropriate insurance program depends on the vehicles you use, who you transport, where you operate, how drivers are hired, whether passengers require assistance, and the contracts your company accepts. That is why an NEMT operation should not be treated like a generic commercial auto account.What insurance does an NEMT business need?Commercial Auto Liability Commercial auto liability is a core component of most NEMT insurance programs. It can help address covered bodily injury or property damage claims resulting from the operation of insured vehicles. The vehicles, passenger capacity, operating radius, driver history and use of each vehicle can all affect the insurance review. Physical Damage Your vehicles are essential business assets. Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles against covered collision and comprehensive losses such as theft, vandalism, fire, weather damage and other covered events. Passenger Exposure NEMT businesses carry people. That distinction matters. Passengers may have mobility limitations, use wheelchairs or other equipment, or require assistance entering and exiting a vehicle. An insurance review should account for the passenger exposure created by the services the business actually provides. General Liability Not every business claim begins with a vehicle accident. General liability can help address certain covered third-party bodily injury or property damage claims arising from business operations outside the normal commercial auto exposure. Workers' Compensation Drivers and transportation staff can face workplace injuries while assisting passengers, operating accessibility equipment, entering facilities, loading mobility devices or performing other duties. Workers' compensation should be reviewed based on the company's employees, state requirements and operational structure. Umbrella or Excess Liability Some NEMT operations, contracts or larger fleets may need liability limits beyond the underlying policies. Umbrella or excess liability may provide additional protection above certain eligible underlying liability policies.Wheelchair transportation changes the riskA wheelchair-accessible transportation company is not simply operating a van with more equipment. The operation may involve: Wheelchair rampsHydraulic liftsSecurement systemsPassenger restraintsMobility devicesDriver assistanceLoading and unloading passengersSpecialized vehicle modifications The condition and use of this equipment can become part of the overall risk. Map the entire passenger journey, from approaching the vehicle to arriving at the destination. Identify who assists the passenger, which equipment is used, and where responsibility changes hands.Medicaid and contract transportationSome NEMT providers perform trips through Medicaid transportation programs, transportation brokers, healthcare networks, facilities or other contractual arrangements. Those contracts can establish insurance requirements that go beyond simply having a commercial auto policy. Your operation may need to provide certificates of insurance or demonstrate particular liability limits before a contract can be activated or renewed. Requirements can vary by state, program, broker and contract. Compare each written insurance requirement with the declarations, coverage forms, and endorsements in the actual policy. A certificate alone does not resolve every coverage question.What affects the cost of NEMT insurance?NEMT insurance pricing is not determined by one factor. Insurers may consider: Number of vehiclesVehicle typePassenger capacityVehicle age and valueWheelchair accessibilityOperating radiusStates of operationNumber of driversDriver experienceMotor vehicle recordsLoss historyAnnual mileageType of passengers transportedContractsHours of operationBusiness experienceCoverage limits The goal should not be to find an insurance policy based on one generic price. The goal is to build an NEMT insurance program that reflects the operation being insured.Starting an NEMT business?Insurance should be part of the business planning process. Before accepting transportation contracts, understand what your vehicles will be used for and what coverage those contracts may require. Questions to document before reviewing coverage: What type of passengers will you transport?Will you provide wheelchair transportation?How many vehicles will you operate?What vehicles are you purchasing?How many passengers can each vehicle carry?Will transportation be private-pay, Medicaid, facility-based or contract work?How far will your vehicles travel?Will you cross state lines?Who will drive?Do your drivers assist passengers?Do you currently have contracts requiring specific insurance limits? Those answers help move the conversation from “I need commercial auto insurance” to a real NEMT insurance review.Growing NEMT fleetsA transportation company with one vehicle has a different insurance challenge from a company operating fifteen. Growth can add: More vehiclesMore driversMore passengersMore facilitiesMore contractsHigher mileageAdditional certificatesMore claims exposureAdditional management responsibilities Insurance should be reviewed as the operation changes. Compare the current operation with the description used when the policies were issued. A new service area, additional passenger assistance, or a larger fleet can change the questions that need to be reviewed.Key takeaways for NEMT operatorsYour passengers depend on your business to get them where they need to go. Your business depends on the vehicles and people that make those trips possible. A useful review connects the coverage documents to the entire transportation operation. Vehicles. Passengers. Drivers. Contracts. Business risk.Coverage comparisonNEMT coverage questions at a glanceSituationReview areaQuestion to askVehicle accidentCommercial auto liabilityWhich vehicles and passenger transportation uses are described in the policy?Damage to your own vanPhysical damageHow are vehicle value, deductible, and accessibility modifications addressed?Passenger assistanceService responsibilities and coverage wordingHow are boarding, unloading, wheelchair securement, and assistance away from the van treated?Employee injuryWorkers’ compensationAre the duties of drivers and passenger-assistance staff accurately described?A new facility contractPolicy limits and endorsementsDo the written requirements match the coverage actually issued?A practical exampleExample: a wheelchair-accessible van joins the fleetAn operator adds an accessible van to a fleet previously used for ambulatory passengers. Listing the vehicle is only one step. Record the lift or ramp, securement equipment, passenger assistance tasks, seating configuration, and any new facility agreement. Ask how each change is reflected in the policy. This example illustrates a review process; it does not establish whether a particular loss would be covered.Common mistakes to avoidConfusing the passenger benefit with business insuranceMedicaid transportation eligibility and an operator’s commercial insurance are different topics. A covered patient trip does not establish that the operator’s business policy addresses every service it performs.Reviewing only the time spent drivingBoarding, transferring assistance, securing equipment, and leaving the vehicle can introduce questions that are missed when the review starts and ends with a vehicle list.Treating a certificate as the whole policyA certificate summarizes selected information. Review the applicable forms and endorsements when a contract calls for a particular protection.Your document review checklistUse these prompts to organize your documents and identify unanswered questions. Completing the list does not confirm coverage.Mark the items you have reviewedVehicle list and accessibility modifications recordedPassenger assistance duties describedDriver and staff responsibilities documentedFacility or broker requirements collectedPolicy terms compared with actual services0 of 5 items reviewedFrequently asked questionsWhat does NEMT insurance cover?NEMT insurance is not one single coverage. A program may include commercial auto liability, physical damage, general liability, workers' compensation, umbrella or excess liability and other coverage depending on the operation.Do wheelchair transportation companies need special insurance?Wheelchair transportation introduces additional operational considerations including mobility equipment, vehicle modifications, passenger assistance, lifts, ramps and securement systems. These details should be discussed when reviewing coverage.Does Medicaid require NEMT insurance?Medicaid transportation programs and transportation brokers can establish provider and insurance requirements. Requirements vary by state, program and contract, so operators should review the specific requirements that apply to their business.What should a new NEMT business review before its first trip?Document the planned vehicles, passenger capacity, accessibility equipment, driver responsibilities, routes, and contracts. Compare those details with the policy and applicable provider requirements before service begins.What documents help organize an NEMT insurance review?Be prepared to provide information about vehicles, drivers, operating radius, passenger capacity, services, wheelchair accessibility, contracts, loss history and requested coverage limits.Sources and further readingMedicaid’s transportation assurance concerns access to covered care. Provider arrangements and operational requirements should be checked with the relevant state program and contract.Medicaid: assurance of transportationNAIC: small business insuranceThis guide explains general insurance considerations. Policy wording, exclusions, state requirements, and the facts of an operation determine what applies.

NEMT Insurance

A practical guide to insurance considerations for medical transportation vehicles, passengers, drivers, accessibility equipment, and contracts.

Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance

Non-emergency medical transportation businesses do more than move passengers from one address to another.

Your drivers may transport seniors, Medicaid members, passengers using wheelchairs, people traveling to dialysis or therapy appointments, and individuals who need additional assistance entering or exiting a vehicle.

That creates a different risk profile than an ordinary commercial vehicle.

This guide explains the coverage categories, operational details, and contract questions that belong in an NEMT insurance review.

Commercial auto. Passenger exposure. Wheelchair transportation. Drivers. Contracts. Business liability.

One insurance conversation.

What is NEMT insurance?

NEMT insurance is commercial insurance structured around businesses providing non-emergency medical transportation.

It may apply to operations such as:

Non-emergency medical transportation
Wheelchair transportation
Ambulette services
Senior transportation
Medicaid transportation
Dialysis transportation
Medical appointment transportation
Mobility-assisted transportation
Private-pay medical transportation

The appropriate insurance program depends on the vehicles you use, who you transport, where you operate, how drivers are hired, whether passengers require assistance, and the contracts your company accepts.

That is why an NEMT operation should not be treated like a generic commercial auto account.

What insurance does an NEMT business need?
Commercial Auto Liability

Commercial auto liability is a core component of most NEMT insurance programs.

It can help address covered bodily injury or property damage claims resulting from the operation of insured vehicles.

The vehicles, passenger capacity, operating radius, driver history and use of each vehicle can all affect the insurance review.

Physical Damage

Your vehicles are essential business assets.

Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles against covered collision and comprehensive losses such as theft, vandalism, fire, weather damage and other covered events.

Passenger Exposure

NEMT businesses carry people.

That distinction matters.

Passengers may have mobility limitations, use wheelchairs or other equipment, or require assistance entering and exiting a vehicle.

An insurance review should account for the passenger exposure created by the services the business actually provides.

General Liability

Not every business claim begins with a vehicle accident.

General liability can help address certain covered third-party bodily injury or property damage claims arising from business operations outside the normal commercial auto exposure.

Workers' Compensation

Drivers and transportation staff can face workplace injuries while assisting passengers, operating accessibility equipment, entering facilities, loading mobility devices or performing other duties.

Workers' compensation should be reviewed based on the company's employees, state requirements and operational structure.

Umbrella or Excess Liability

Some NEMT operations, contracts or larger fleets may need liability limits beyond the underlying policies.

Umbrella or excess liability may provide additional protection above certain eligible underlying liability policies.

Wheelchair transportation changes the risk

A wheelchair-accessible transportation company is not simply operating a van with more equipment.

The operation may involve:

Wheelchair ramps
Hydraulic lifts
Securement systems
Passenger restraints
Mobility devices
Driver assistance
Loading and unloading passengers
Specialized vehicle modifications

The condition and use of this equipment can become part of the overall risk.

Map the entire passenger journey, from approaching the vehicle to arriving at the destination. Identify who assists the passenger, which equipment is used, and where responsibility changes hands.

Medicaid and contract transportation

Some NEMT providers perform trips through Medicaid transportation programs, transportation brokers, healthcare networks, facilities or other contractual arrangements.

Those contracts can establish insurance requirements that go beyond simply having a commercial auto policy.

Your operation may need to provide certificates of insurance or demonstrate particular liability limits before a contract can be activated or renewed.

Requirements can vary by state, program, broker and contract.

Compare each written insurance requirement with the declarations, coverage forms, and endorsements in the actual policy. A certificate alone does not resolve every coverage question.

What affects the cost of NEMT insurance?

NEMT insurance pricing is not determined by one factor.

Insurers may consider:

Number of vehicles
Vehicle type
Passenger capacity
Vehicle age and value
Wheelchair accessibility
Operating radius
States of operation
Number of drivers
Driver experience
Motor vehicle records
Loss history
Annual mileage
Type of passengers transported
Contracts
Hours of operation
Business experience
Coverage limits

The goal should not be to find an insurance policy based on one generic price.

The goal is to build an NEMT insurance program that reflects the operation being insured.

Starting an NEMT business?

Insurance should be part of the business planning process.

Before accepting transportation contracts, understand what your vehicles will be used for and what coverage those contracts may require.

Questions to document before reviewing coverage:

What type of passengers will you transport?
Will you provide wheelchair transportation?
How many vehicles will you operate?
What vehicles are you purchasing?
How many passengers can each vehicle carry?
Will transportation be private-pay, Medicaid, facility-based or contract work?
How far will your vehicles travel?
Will you cross state lines?
Who will drive?
Do your drivers assist passengers?
Do you currently have contracts requiring specific insurance limits?

Those answers help move the conversation from “I need commercial auto insurance” to a real NEMT insurance review.

Growing NEMT fleets

A transportation company with one vehicle has a different insurance challenge from a company operating fifteen.

Growth can add:

More vehicles
More drivers
More passengers
More facilities
More contracts
Higher mileage
Additional certificates
More claims exposure
Additional management responsibilities

Insurance should be reviewed as the operation changes.

Compare the current operation with the description used when the policies were issued. A new service area, additional passenger assistance, or a larger fleet can change the questions that need to be reviewed.

Key takeaways for NEMT operators

Your passengers depend on your business to get them where they need to go.

Your business depends on the vehicles and people that make those trips possible.

A useful review connects the coverage documents to the entire transportation operation.

Vehicles.

Passengers.

Drivers.

Contracts.

Business risk.

Coverage comparison
NEMT coverage questions at a glance
Situation	Review area	Question to ask
Vehicle accident	Commercial auto liability	Which vehicles and passenger transportation uses are described in the policy?
Damage to your own van	Physical damage	How are vehicle value, deductible, and accessibility modifications addressed?
Passenger assistance	Service responsibilities and coverage wording	How are boarding, unloading, wheelchair securement, and assistance away from the van treated?
Employee injury	Workers’ compensation	Are the duties of drivers and passenger-assistance staff accurately described?
A new facility contract	Policy limits and endorsements	Do the written requirements match the coverage actually issued?
A practical example
Example: a wheelchair-accessible van joins the fleet

An operator adds an accessible van to a fleet previously used for ambulatory passengers. Listing the vehicle is only one step. Record the lift or ramp, securement equipment, passenger assistance tasks, seating configuration, and any new facility agreement. Ask how each change is reflected in the policy. This example illustrates a review process; it does not establish whether a particular loss would be covered.

Common mistakes to avoid
Confusing the passenger benefit with business insurance

Medicaid transportation eligibility and an operator’s commercial insurance are different topics. A covered patient trip does not establish that the operator’s business policy addresses every service it performs.

Reviewing only the time spent driving

Boarding, transferring assistance, securing equipment, and leaving the vehicle can introduce questions that are missed when the review starts and ends with a vehicle list.

Treating a certificate as the whole policy

A certificate summarizes selected information. Review the applicable forms and endorsements when a contract calls for a particular protection.

@graph.description: Learn how passenger capacity, routes, airport access, drivers, and contracts affect shuttle insurance reviews for hotel, employee, church, and group transportation.

mainEntity.name: What insurance does a shuttle business need?

acceptedAnswer.text: Coverage may include commercial auto liability, physical damage, general liability, workers' compensation, umbrella or excess liability and other coverage depending on the operation.

mainEntity.name: Is airport shuttle insurance different from regular commercial auto?

acceptedAnswer.text: It can be. Passenger transportation, airport operations, routes, vehicle capacity and contractual requirements can create considerations not present in a standard commercial vehicle account.

mainEntity.name: Does seating capacity affect shuttle insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Passenger capacity can affect underwriting and may affect regulatory financial responsibility requirements for certain operations.

mainEntity.name: What makes employee shuttle transportation different?

acceptedAnswer.text: Identify the vehicle owner, driver employer, passengers, routes, and transportation contract. A service carrying another company’s employees can have a different structure from an employer moving its own workers.

mainEntity.name: Can a new shuttle company get insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Potentially. Available options depend on the vehicles, drivers, routes, business plan, experience and insurance market.

nojs.mainText:
Home
Specialty Transportation
Shuttle Insurance
Shuttle Insurance

Understand the coverage questions behind airport, hotel, employee, church, daycare, and group passenger transportation.

Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance

Airport shuttle.

Hotel shuttle.

Employee transportation.

Church transportation.

Daycare transportation.

Private group transportation.

The destination may change, but one thing does not:

Your business is responsible for passengers while they are being transported.

This guide explains how vehicles, seating capacity, drivers, routes, contracts, and passenger responsibilities shape a shuttle insurance review.

Shuttle operations are different from ordinary commercial auto

A commercial van used by a contractor to carry equipment does not create the same exposure as a van carrying passengers.

For shuttle companies, the people inside the vehicle are a central part of the risk.

Insurance considerations may include:

Vehicle seating capacity
Number of passengers
Type of passengers
Driver qualifications
Frequency of trips
Regular routes
Airport operations
Hotel contracts
Employee transportation contracts
Church transportation
Daycare transportation
Interstate operations
Vehicle ownership

That makes shuttle insurance a specialty transportation conversation.

Airport shuttle insurance

Airport shuttle businesses may operate on tight schedules with frequent pickups and drop-offs.

Vehicles may spend significant time:

In airport traffic
At terminals
At hotels
On highways
In parking and loading zones
Transporting luggage
Carrying multiple passengers

The insurance review should reflect the frequency and nature of those operations rather than simply classifying the vehicle as a van or bus.

Hotel shuttle insurance

Hotels and independent transportation providers may offer scheduled or on-demand shuttle service between hotels, airports, entertainment areas and other destinations.

When transportation is provided as part of a larger service or commercial arrangement, operators should understand how that transportation is classified and what insurance requirements apply.

Document the vehicle use and passenger responsibilities associated with the service, including who owns the vehicle and who employs the driver.

Employee transportation insurance

Businesses sometimes transport workers between:

Parking areas and job sites
Facilities
Warehouses
Hotels
Construction projects
Factories
Airports
Transit stations
Remote work locations

Employee shuttle operations may involve repeated routes and high passenger frequency.

Coverage should be evaluated around the actual transportation arrangement, vehicle capacity and operation.

Church and group transportation

Churches, nonprofit organizations and community groups may operate vans or buses for events, services and group activities.

Nonprofit status by itself does not eliminate transportation risk.

The insurance review should consider who owns the vehicle, who drives it, how transportation is funded, seating capacity, where trips occur and how frequently passengers are transported.

Daycare and child transportation

Transporting children creates responsibilities that should be evaluated carefully.

Daycare transportation may involve:

Pickup and drop-off
Scheduled routes
Multiple stops
Passenger supervision
Vans or buses
Special loading procedures
Contracts or licensing requirements

Insurance requirements can vary by jurisdiction and operation.

Review the vehicle use, passenger supervision, and written transportation responsibilities together.

Commercial auto and passenger liability

Shuttle insurance often begins with commercial auto liability.

But passenger transportation requires a deeper review than simply listing vehicles.

For qualifying interstate for-hire passenger carriers, federal financial responsibility requirements can depend on the highest seating capacity of vehicles in the fleet.

Operators should also consider applicable state requirements and contractual limits.

Verify which rules apply to the actual operation before treating a regulatory minimum as the right limit for the business.

Physical damage

Your shuttle vehicles generate revenue.

Physical damage coverage can help protect insured vehicles against covered collision and comprehensive losses.

For larger fleets, vehicle values, deductibles and replacement considerations should be reviewed together rather than one vehicle at a time.

General liability

A shuttle company also has business exposures away from the driver's seat.

General liability may help address certain covered claims involving business operations that fall outside normal commercial auto liability.

Workers' compensation

Drivers and other employees may face injuries while performing their jobs.

Workers' compensation requirements vary, but it should be considered as part of the overall insurance program.

What shapes shuttle insurance cost?

Pricing may be influenced by:

Passenger capacity
Number of vehicles
Vehicle type
Vehicle value
Driver records
Years in business
Claims history
Routes
Annual mileage
Operating radius
Interstate travel
Airport exposure
Contracts
Passenger type
Coverage limits
Deductibles
Build insurance around the route

The right question is not:

“What does shuttle insurance cost?”
It is:
“What does this shuttle operation actually do?”

A three-vehicle hotel shuttle serving one airport has a different risk profile from an employee transportation company operating twenty vehicles across several states.

Start with an accurate description of the operation.

Then compare the insurance documents with that description.

Coverage comparison
Compare the shuttle operation before comparing coverage
Situation	Review area	Question to ask
Airport or hotel shuttle	Frequent stops, luggage, terminal access	Which vehicles, drivers, routes, and access agreements are involved?
Employee shuttle	Vehicle ownership and contract responsibilities	Who employs the driver, owns the vehicle, and organizes the transportation?
Church or community group	Volunteer drivers and occasional trips	Are driver arrangements, trip frequency, and passenger capacity documented?
Daycare transportation	Passenger supervision and loading procedures	Which staff duties, stops, and applicable licensing requirements need review?
Interstate passenger service	Applicable registration and insurance rules	Does the specific service fall within federal passenger-carrier requirements or an exception?
A practical example
Example: a hotel shuttle begins employee transportation

A hotel’s shuttle begins carrying a nearby business’s staff during shift changes. The vehicle may be unchanged, but the passengers, frequency, contract, and responsibility for transportation have changed. Update the route description and gather the new agreement before assuming the original insurance arrangement fits the additional work. The example is a planning prompt, not a coverage determination.

Common mistakes to avoid
Using today’s passenger count as the seating capacity

A partially occupied van can still have the same designed seating configuration. Record the actual vehicle configuration instead of describing only the number of riders on a typical trip.

Assuming a free ride has no insurance implications

Transportation offered as part of another business service still needs an accurate description. Document how the service is arranged and discuss how that arrangement affects the review.

Ignoring the driver arrangement

Employees, volunteers, and contracted transportation providers can create different operational structures. Keep the vehicle owner and driver employer clear.

Your document review checklist

Use these prompts to organize your documents and identify unanswered questions. Completing the list does not confirm coverage.

Mark the items you have reviewed
Seating capacity and vehicle configuration recordedVehicle owner and driver employer identifiedRegular and occasional routes documentedAirport, hotel, or organization agreements collectedApplicable passenger-carrier rules checked
0 of 5 items reviewed

Is airport shuttle insurance different from regular commercial auto?
Does seating capacity affect shuttle insurance?
What makes employee shuttle transportation different?
Can a new shuttle company get insurance?
Sources and further reading

FMCSA lists federal financial-responsibility requirements for qualifying passenger carriers. Applicability depends on the operation; state rules, exceptions, and contract requirements also need review.

FMCSA: insurance filing requirements
NAIC: small business insurance

This guide explains general insurance considerations. Policy wording, exclusions, state requirements, and the facts of an operation determine what applies.

mainEntity.name: Is specialty transportation insurance different from regular commercial auto?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Passenger transportation, customer vehicles, medical transportation, towing and contracts can require a broader review than standard commercial auto.

mainEntity.name: Does every transportation company need passenger liability?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Passenger liability concerns operations that carry people. Towing, vehicle transport and delivery businesses may have different priorities.

mainEntity.name: Can Motive review insurance requirements in a contract?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Motive can help review required limits, certificates, endorsements and other insurance terms before coverage decisions are made.

mainEntity.name: What information should I have ready for a quote?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prepare your business, vehicle and driver details, service area, passengers or property transported, contracts, claims history and current insurance.

mainEntity.name: Can my insurance change as my transportation business grows?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. More vehicles, drivers, services or operating areas can change your exposures and coverage options.

mainEntity.name: Is specialty transportation insurance different from regular commercial auto?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Passenger transportation, customer vehicles, medical transportation, towing and contracts can require a broader review than standard commercial auto.

mainEntity.name: Does every transportation company need passenger liability?

acceptedAnswer.text: Not always. Passenger liability concerns operations that carry people. Towing, vehicle transport and delivery businesses may have different priorities.

mainEntity.name: Can Motive review insurance requirements in a contract?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. Motive can help review required limits, certificates, endorsements and other insurance terms before coverage decisions are made.

mainEntity.name: What information should I have ready for a quote?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prepare your business, vehicle and driver details, service area, passengers or property transported, contracts, claims history and current insurance.

mainEntity.name: Can my insurance change as my transportation business grows?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes. More vehicles, drivers, services or operating areas can change your exposures and coverage options.

What Type of Transportation Business Do You Operate?

Not every transportation company faces the same risks. Choose the operation closest to your business to explore the coverage questions to review.
