Understand passenger liability, wheelchair equipment, driver qualifications and contract requirements for non-emergency medical transportation.

Learn more about NEMT insurance →

Learn more about Shuttle Insurance →

Learn more about Executive Transportation Insurance →
Towing and Roadside Assistance

Learn how tow truck, on-hook, garagekeepers and roadside coverage relate to customer vehicles, recovery work and storage.

Learn more about Towing and Roadside Insurance →
Vehicle Transport and Vehicle Movement

Understand truck, trailer and cargo coverage questions when customer vehicles are hauled, relocated or temporarily stored.

Learn more about Vehicle Transport Insurance →
Specialty Transportation Insurance Is More Than Commercial Auto

Commercial auto is one part of the picture. Depending on your operation, review these coverage and contract questions together.

Commercial Auto Liability
Physical Damage
Passenger Liability
General Liability
Workers’ Compensation
Hired and Non-Owned Auto

What Determines Your Transportation Insurance Needs?

Insurance companies review the operation, not just the vehicle.

Vehicles

The number, type, age and value of your vehicles affect coverage and pricing.

Drivers

Driving history, experience, qualifications and driver numbers affect underwriting.

Passengers or Property

Transporting people creates different risks than moving vehicles, equipment or customer property.

Operating Area

Routes, operating radius, service territory and interstate work can influence requirements.

Contracts

Customers may require specific liability limits, documentation or endorsements.

Business Growth

Additional vehicles, drivers, locations or services can change existing coverage needs.

Before You Accept a Transportation Contract

A contract can require more than proof of insurance. Before signing, compare the requested coverage with your existing policies.

Liability limits
Passenger liability
Additional insured endorsements
Certificates of Insurance
Workers’ compensation
Commercial auto limits
Cargo or property coverage
Vehicle-specific requirements

Review the requirements before work begins so potential gaps can be identified early.

Coverage that suited one vehicle may not fit several vehicles and multiple drivers. As your business grows, review:

Vehicle schedules
Driver lists
Liability limits
Claims history
Physical damage coverage
Passenger exposure
Contracts
Certificates
Fleet administration

Review coverage when vehicles, services or contracts change.

raw.text: Tow Truck InsuranceUnderstand the coverage questions for your tow truck, customer vehicles, roadside work, equipment, and storage operations. The insurance needs of a single light-duty rollback operation may be significantly different from a towing company operating wreckers, storage lots and heavy recovery equipment.Commercial auto liabilityTow trucks spend significant time on public roads. Commercial auto liability can help protect the business when an insured vehicle is involved in a covered accident causing bodily injury or property damage. Underwriters may consider: Truck typeTruck weightOperating radiusTowing radiusDriver recordsYears in businessClaims historyNumber of trucksTypes of vehicles towedContractsHours of operationRoadside exposureOn-hook towing coverageOne of the most important distinctions in tow truck insurance involves the customer's vehicle. On-hook towing coverage can help protect a customer's vehicle from certain covered damage while it is being towed by the insured tow truck. That is a different exposure from damage involving your own tow truck. A towing company should understand: Its on-hook limitDeductibleCovered causes of lossVehicle types handledMaximum value of vehicles towedTerritoryPolicy exclusions If your company occasionally tows expensive vehicles, the limit should be evaluated against the actual vehicles you handle.Garagekeepers coverageWhat happens when the customer's vehicle is no longer attached to the tow truck? Towing companies that store, park or otherwise take custody of customer vehicles may need to review garagekeepers coverage. Garagekeepers and on-hook towing address different portions of the risk. This distinction becomes especially important for towing operations with storage yards or facilities.Physical damageTow trucks and recovery equipment can represent a major capital investment. Physical damage coverage can help protect insured trucks against covered collision and comprehensive losses. Truck value, attached equipment and aftermarket modifications should be disclosed accurately.General liabilityA towing business can have liabilities that do not arise from driving. General liability may help address certain covered third-party claims connected with business premises and operations outside the normal auto exposure.Workers' compensationTow operators work in difficult environments. Highways. Road shoulders. Accident scenes. Parking lots. Bad weather. Nighttime calls. Vehicle recovery sites. Workers' compensation should be reviewed based on the business's employees and applicable state requirements.Roadside assistance insuranceRoadside businesses may provide more than towing. Services can include: Battery jumpsTire changesFuel deliveryLockoutsWinchingMinor roadside assistance Each service can create its own operational exposure. Tell the insurer what the business actually does. Do not describe an operation as “towing only” if technicians are regularly performing additional roadside services.Vehicle recovery operationsRecovery work can involve damaged vehicles, unusual locations, specialized equipment and more complex working conditions. Operations involving heavy recovery, rotators, commercial vehicles or specialized equipment should be explained clearly during underwriting.What affects tow truck insurance cost?Factors may include: Number of tow trucksType of trucksTruck valueDriver experienceMotor vehicle recordsClaims historyOperating radiusType of towingRoadside servicesStorage operationsPolice or municipal contractsVehicle values handledOn-hook limitsGaragekeepers limitsHours of operationCoverage limitsDeductiblesTowing insurance should follow the vehicle from pickup to releaseThink about the complete chain. Your tow truck arrives. The vehicle is connected. The vehicle is transported. The vehicle may be stored. The vehicle is eventually released. Different insurance coverages can apply at different stages. A complete towing insurance review considers each stage, rather than assuming one commercial auto coverage answers every question. Document the complete chain of responsibility, including any storage or subcontracted work.Coverage comparisonFollow the customer vehicle through the operationSituationReview areaQuestion to askDriving the tow truckCommercial auto liabilityWhich insured vehicles, drivers, and uses are described?Damage to the tow truckPhysical damageHow are the truck, recovery equipment, value, and deductible addressed?Customer vehicle being towedOn-hook or applicable customer-vehicle coverageWhat causes of loss, vehicle values, limits, and exclusions apply?Customer vehicle held at a yardGaragekeepers or applicable custody coverageWhich locations and custody arrangements are addressed?Roadside servicesThe relevant policy forms for those activitiesAre lockouts, jumps, tire changes, winching, and fuel delivery accurately described?A practical exampleExample: a towing company adds overnight storageA towing operator begins holding recovered vehicles overnight instead of delivering every vehicle directly to a repair shop. Record the storage location, maximum number of vehicles, security arrangements, and maximum combined value. Ask how the policy addresses that custody period. The coverage question changes when the customer’s vehicle leaves the tow truck, even though the customer and towing job remain the same.Common mistakes to avoidTreating on-hook and storage protection as interchangeableRead the actual covered activities and locations. Product names and policy wording vary; Progressive notes different terminology in Texas and Virginia. A label alone does not establish when protection applies.Understating the value of customer vehiclesUse the highest-value vehicles the business actually handles, not only the average local tow, when evaluating limit questions.Leaving roadside work out of the descriptionA towing-only description can miss battery jumps, tire changes, lockouts, and other services performed during the same shift.Your document review checklistUse these prompts to organize your documents and identify unanswered questions. Completing the list does not confirm coverage.Mark the items you have reviewedAll towing and roadside services listedTruck and recovery equipment values recordedMaximum customer vehicle values identifiedStorage locations and custody arrangements documentedRelevant limits, deductibles, and exclusions compared0 of 5 items reviewedFrequently asked questionsWhat insurance does a tow truck company need?A towing operation may need commercial auto liability, physical damage, on-hook towing, garagekeepers, general liability, workers' compensation and other coverage depending on its operation.What is on-hook towing insurance?On-hook coverage can help address certain covered damage to a customer's vehicle while that vehicle is being towed by an insured tow truck.What is the difference between on-hook and garagekeepers coverage?On-hook coverage generally relates to a customer's vehicle while being towed. Garagekeepers coverage may apply to customer vehicles held in the business's care at a location or storage facility, subject to policy terms.Does roadside assistance need commercial insurance?Businesses performing roadside assistance should disclose those services when applying for insurance so the operation can be evaluated accurately.What should a new towing company document before starting?Prepare the truck and equipment schedule, services offered, towing radius, driver information, maximum customer vehicle values, storage arrangements, and contract requirements. Identify where each stage of work is addressed in the policy.Sources and further readingInsurer explanations distinguish towing-related customer vehicle coverage from protection for vehicles held at a business location. The policy’s definitions and terms control; terminology can vary by state.Progressive: on-hook towing coverageProgressive: garagekeepers coverageNAIC: small business insuranceThis guide explains general insurance considerations. Policy wording, exclusions, state requirements, and the facts of an operation determine what applies.

mainEntity.name: What insurance does a tow truck company need?

acceptedAnswer.text: A towing operation may need commercial auto liability, physical damage, on-hook towing, garagekeepers, general liability, workers' compensation and other coverage depending on its operation.

mainEntity.name: What is on-hook towing insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: On-hook coverage can help address certain covered damage to a customer's vehicle while that vehicle is being towed by an insured tow truck.

mainEntity.name: What is the difference between on-hook and garagekeepers coverage?

acceptedAnswer.text: On-hook coverage generally relates to a customer's vehicle while being towed. Garagekeepers coverage may apply to customer vehicles held in the business's care at a location or storage facility, subject to policy terms.

mainEntity.name: Does roadside assistance need commercial insurance?

acceptedAnswer.text: Businesses performing roadside assistance should disclose those services when applying for insurance so the operation can be evaluated accurately.

mainEntity.name: What should a new towing company document before starting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prepare the truck and equipment schedule, services offered, towing radius, driver information, maximum customer vehicle values, storage arrangements, and contract requirements. Identify where each stage of work is addressed in the policy.

mainEntity.name: What should a new towing company document before starting?

acceptedAnswer.text: Prepare the truck and equipment schedule, services offered, towing radius, driver information, maximum customer vehicle values, storage arrangements, and contract requirements. Identify where each stage of work is addressed in the policy.

Home
Specialty Transportation
Tow Truck Insurance
Tow Truck Insurance

Understand the coverage questions for your tow truck, customer vehicles, roadside work, equipment, and storage operations.

Insurance guide · Updated November 2, 2026 · By Motive Insurance

A towing business has an unusual responsibility.

You are operating your own commercial vehicle while taking responsibility for somebody else's vehicle.

That creates two separate questions:

This guide separates the tow truck’s own coverage from the coverage questions surrounding customer vehicles, roadside services, and storage.

Who needs tow truck insurance?

Tow truck insurance may apply to businesses providing:

Local towing
Roadside assistance
Vehicle recovery
Accident towing
Private-property towing
Police rotation towing
Dealer towing
Repossession-related towing
Heavy-duty towing
Light-duty towing
Winching
Jump starts
Lockout service
Tire changes
Fuel delivery
Vehicle storage

Different services create different exposures.

The insurance needs of a single light-duty rollback operation may be significantly different from a towing company operating wreckers, storage lots and heavy recovery equipment.

Commercial auto liability

Tow trucks spend significant time on public roads.

Commercial auto liability can help protect the business when an insured vehicle is involved in a covered accident causing bodily injury or property damage.

Underwriters may consider:

Truck type
Truck weight
Operating radius
Towing radius
Driver records
Years in business
Claims history
Number of trucks
Types of vehicles towed
Contracts
Hours of operation
Roadside exposure
On-hook towing coverage

One of the most important distinctions in tow truck insurance involves the customer's vehicle.

On-hook towing coverage can help protect a customer's vehicle from certain covered damage while it is being towed by the insured tow truck.

That is a different exposure from damage involving your own tow truck.

A towing company should understand:

Its on-hook limit
Deductible
Covered causes of loss
Vehicle types handled
Maximum value of vehicles towed
Territory
Policy exclusions

If your company occasionally tows expensive vehicles, the limit should be evaluated against the actual vehicles you handle.

Garagekeepers coverage

What happens when the customer's vehicle is no longer attached to the tow truck?

Towing companies that store, park or otherwise take custody of customer vehicles may need to review garagekeepers coverage.

Garagekeepers and on-hook towing address different portions of the risk.

This distinction becomes especially important for towing operations with storage yards or facilities.

Physical damage

Tow trucks and recovery equipment can represent a major capital investment.

Physical damage coverage can help protect insured trucks against covered collision and comprehensive losses.

Truck value, attached equipment and aftermarket modifications should be disclosed accurately.

General liability

A towing business can have liabilities that do not arise from driving.

General liability may help address certain covered third-party claims connected with business premises and operations outside the normal auto exposure.

Workers' compensation

Tow operators work in difficult environments.

Highways.

Road shoulders.

Accident scenes.

Parking lots.

Bad weather.

Nighttime calls.

Vehicle recovery sites.

Workers' compensation should be reviewed based on the business's employees and applicable state requirements.

Roadside assistance insurance

Roadside businesses may provide more than towing.

Services can include:

Battery jumps
Tire changes
Fuel delivery
Lockouts
Winching
Minor roadside assistance

Each service can create its own operational exposure.

Tell the insurer what the business actually does.

Do not describe an operation as “towing only” if technicians are regularly performing additional roadside services.

Vehicle recovery operations

Recovery work can involve damaged vehicles, unusual locations, specialized equipment and more complex working conditions.

Operations involving heavy recovery, rotators, commercial vehicles or specialized equipment should be explained clearly during underwriting.

What affects tow truck insurance cost?

Factors may include:

Number of tow trucks
Type of trucks
Truck value
Driver experience
Motor vehicle records
Claims history
Operating radius
Type of towing
Roadside services
Storage operations
Police or municipal contracts
Vehicle values handled
On-hook limits
Garagekeepers limits
Hours of operation
Coverage limits
Deductibles
Towing insurance should follow the vehicle from pickup to release

Think about the complete chain.

Your tow truck arrives.

The vehicle is connected.

The vehicle is transported.

The vehicle may be stored.

The vehicle is eventually released.

Different insurance coverages can apply at different stages.

A complete towing insurance review considers each stage, rather than assuming one commercial auto coverage answers every question.

Document the complete chain of responsibility, including any storage or subcontracted work.

Coverage comparison
Follow the customer vehicle through the operation
Situation	Review area	Question to ask
Driving the tow truck	Commercial auto liability	Which insured vehicles, drivers, and uses are described?
Damage to the tow truck	Physical damage	How are the truck, recovery equipment, value, and deductible addressed?
Customer vehicle being towed	On-hook or applicable customer-vehicle coverage	What causes of loss, vehicle values, limits, and exclusions apply?
Customer vehicle held at a yard	Garagekeepers or applicable custody coverage	Which locations and custody arrangements are addressed?
Roadside services	The relevant policy forms for those activities	Are lockouts, jumps, tire changes, winching, and fuel delivery accurately described?
A practical example
Example: a towing company adds overnight storage

A towing operator begins holding recovered vehicles overnight instead of delivering every vehicle directly to a repair shop. Record the storage location, maximum number of vehicles, security arrangements, and maximum combined value. Ask how the policy addresses that custody period. The coverage question changes when the customer’s vehicle leaves the tow truck, even though the customer and towing job remain the same.

Common mistakes to avoid
Treating on-hook and storage protection as interchangeable

Read the actual covered activities and locations. Product names and policy wording vary; Progressive notes different terminology in Texas and Virginia. A label alone does not establish when protection applies.

Understating the value of customer vehicles

Use the highest-value vehicles the business actually handles, not only the average local tow, when evaluating limit questions.

Leaving roadside work out of the description

A towing-only description can miss battery jumps, tire changes, lockouts, and other services performed during the same shift.

Your document review checklist

Use these prompts to organize your documents and identify unanswered questions. Completing the list does not confirm coverage.

Mark the items you have reviewed
All towing and roadside services listedTruck and recovery equipment values recordedMaximum customer vehicle values identifiedStorage locations and custody arrangements documentedRelevant limits, deductibles, and exclusions compared
0 of 5 items reviewed
Frequently asked questions
What insurance does a tow truck company need?
What is on-hook towing insurance?
What is the difference between on-hook and garagekeepers coverage?
Does roadside assistance need commercial insurance?
What should a new towing company document before starting?
Sources and further reading

Insurer explanations distinguish towing-related customer vehicle coverage from protection for vehicles held at a business location. The policy’s definitions and terms control; terminology can vary by state.

Progressive: on-hook towing coverage
Progressive: garagekeepers coverage
NAIC: small business insurance

This guide explains general insurance considerations. Policy wording, exclusions, state requirements, and the facts of an operation determine what applies.
